items.title: Simple beats theoretical
items.text: Choose openings built on sound principles rather than endless variations. You leave the opening with confidence and without memory slips.
items.check: Fine advice for club players. At master level theory matters more.

examples.caption: White to move (move 9). White has built the quiet Italian set-up: c3, d3, h3 and Re1, and now brings the last knight out with Nbd2. Every move follows a simple plan, with no sharp theory to remember. White is slightly ahead.
examples.source: Caruana, Fabiano vs Nakamura, Hikaru, Norway Chess, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2024-open/round-1/I9TLGEOt/Dlc92a2Q)

items.title: A doubled pawn is not always weak
items.text: It becomes a problem when it is isolated and cannot be defended. If it takes squares from the opponent and controls the centre, it can be very useful.
items.check: Checked: the weakness usually comes from isolation, blocked pawns or lost flexibility, not from the doubling itself.

examples.caption: White to move (move 15). White has doubled c-pawns, but c3 and c4 support d4 and e4, so White holds the centre and Black has little space. The position is equal, so the doubled pawns are not a problem here.
examples.source: Praggnanandhaa vs Gukesh, Tata Steel Masters 2025, round 8 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-chess-2025-masters/round-8/ywc5BNQT/t9KDQlLY)

items.title: Be flexible in the opening
items.text: You do not have to follow the main line to get a good position. A less common move order makes your opponent think for themselves from the start.
items.check: Checked: works only if you understand the position. Sound principles still come first.

examples.caption: White to move (move 3). After 2...a6 White skips the main-line 3.d4 and plays 3.c4, a less common set-up, so Black has to think from the start. White is slightly better, so the unusual move order is fully sound.
examples.source: Fabiano Caruana vs Teimour Radjabov, Round 7: Fabiano Caruana - Teimour Radjabov, 2022 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-candidates-tournament-2022/round-7/OFBhwamI/d7lcMo4O)

items.title: Control the centre in the opening
items.text: Fight for the four central squares with pawns and pieces from the first moves. Central pieces cover the most squares and give you freedom to move.

examples.caption: White to move (move 3). Black has only one pawn in the centre. White fights for the central squares at once with 3.d4, attacking the e5 pawn. It is the strongest move, ahead of quieter developing moves, and White is clearly better.
examples.source: Morphy vs Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard, Paris 1858 ("Opera Game"; moves from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opera_Game)

items.title: Develop your minor pieces
items.text: Bring your knights and bishops into the game early, each to a useful square. Do not move the same piece twice without a reason.

examples.caption: White to move (move 6). Black's knights and bishop are still at home. White develops the bishop to its best square: 6.Bc4 hits f7. Qb3 is also strong, but Bc4 is nearly as good, and White is much better.
examples.source: Morphy vs Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard, Paris 1858 ("Opera Game"; moves from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opera_Game)

items.title: Be economical with your moves
items.text: Make every move the most active option and skip useless manoeuvres. Lost time in the opening hands your opponent a lead in development.
items.check: Checked: this is the idea of tempo.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 10). Black already spent a move on ...h6; now ...g6 is another pawn move while White's pieces are out. ...Na5 is more accurate and keeps the position about equal; after 10...g6 White is clearly better. A punished violation: lost time is a lead for the opponent.
examples.source: Caruana, Fabiano vs Firouzja, Alireza, Norway Chess, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2024-open/round-7/4FLBpAW3/gPXBZQj3)

items.title: Castle early
items.text: Do not play recklessly: get your king safe early in the opening by castling, before the middlegame breaks loose.
items.check: Checked: standard and sound. Another lesson: castle short before you start complicated actions or breaks in the centre.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 10). The king is still on e8 and Black can castle. 10...O-O is the strongest move and keeps the position equal. Black played 10...Nf6? instead; after 11.Re1+ the king is stuck in the centre and White is much better.

items.title: Flexible move order: centre and development first
items.text: Do not rush to finish a fixed pawn set-up, such as a pawn triangle. First control the centre and develop your minor pieces. The pawn structure can wait.
items.check: Checked: sound, and it fits the opening principles above.

examples.caption: White to move (move 4). White has played only Nf3, g3 and Bg2: no fixed pawn set-up yet. Now 4.d4 takes the centre and keeps c4 and castling for later. White is slightly better, and this is the strongest move. Pieces and centre first, pawn structure can wait.
examples.source: Harikrishna, Pentala vs Warmerdam, Max, Tata Steel Chess Tournament 2025 Masters, 2025 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-chess-2025-masters/round-4/LatXHomI/6SKhfpLT)

items.title: Pawn support frees your pieces
items.text: A solid pawn defence, such as c6 backing d5, takes defending jobs off your pieces. Once a centre pawn is covered by a pawn, the knight next to it is free to go on the attack.
items.check: Checked: the idea behind the Caro-Kann and Slav set-ups.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 8). The c6 pawn guards d5, so the knight on f6 no longer has to watch that pawn. It can jump to e4 and hit the knight on c3. 8...Ne4 is the strongest move, and White is only slightly better.
examples.source: Sarana vs Fedoseev, Tata Steel Masters 2025 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-chess-2025-masters/round-6/42KuhhJZ/cZzuSrcu)

items.title: Do not bring the queen out too early
items.text: Do not rush the queen to the centre where enemy minor pieces can attack it. You lose tempo moving it again and again.
items.check: Checked: correct for the opening. A queen move can be fine when nothing can hit it. Another lesson repeats this: do not bring the queen out in the first moves; it gets attacked and you lose time moving it again.

examples.caption: White to move (move 7). White's queen came out early with 5.Qxd4, was hit by ...Nc6, went to g4 and was hit again after ...Nxe5, which also won a pawn. White has no minor piece developed and Black's knight is centralised. Black is much better.

items.title: Watch for flank pawns challenging your centre
items.text: Be alert when your opponent tries to trade off your centre pawn with a flank pawn (such as ...c5) and claim the centre. Keep the option of recapturing with a centre pawn of your own.
items.check: Checked: a typical theme (Sicilian, Benoni structures).

examples.caption: White to move (move 6). Black's c-pawn is hitting the d4 centre pawn from the flank. 6.c3 supports d4, so after ...cxd4 White can recapture with the e-pawn (exd4) and keep a pawn in the centre. It is the strongest move, and White is slightly better.
examples.source: Firouzja vs Ding Liren, Norway Chess 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2024-open/round-4/4JSenCaJ/iZ0cIhtU)

items.title: The accordion pawn structure
items.text: In a solid pawn triangle you can sometimes sacrifice or trade a flank pawn and then answer with b4, so that all your pawns link up and cannot be broken.
items.check: Draft: I could not confirm the name "accordion" or this exact idea. It needs a concrete position from Peter before we publish it.

items.title: Attack weak, misplaced pieces at once
items.text: Spot an opponent's misplaced piece, such as a knight on c6 played too early, and put maximum pressure on it with active pieces, for example a bishop on b5 and a queen on a4.
items.check: Checked: sound. Check that the attack does not leave your own pieces loose. Another lesson: look for undefended squares and trap or force a defence with a knight or pawn thrust against a vulnerable knight or cut-off piece. Also covers: when the opponent brings a queen or knight to the centre too early, upset it at once by attacking it with minor pieces or pawns. They lose tempi relocating it. Softened: make sure your attacking move also develops you, or you lose the tempo battle yourself.

examples.caption: White to move (move 8). Black's early ...Nc6 blocked a check, so it is pinned to the king by the queen on a4. 8.Ng5 also unmasks the Bg2. The game went 8...Nb6 9.Bxc6+ bxc6 10.Qxc6+, winning a pawn. The position is about equal, so the pressure wins material but Black keeps compensation.
examples.source: Caruana, Fabiano vs Wei, Yi, FIDE Candidates Tournament 2026, 2026 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-candidates-2026-open/round-3/SDizieNR/8EWUBjpx)

items.title: Win back the sacrificed pawn
items.text: If you sacrifice a pawn, play for the compensation (lead in development, initiative). Winning the pawn back is often a good option, but it is not a goal in itself.
items.check: Softened: "absolute priority" is too strong. If your compensation (initiative, development) is worth more than the pawn, keep playing for that. Do not let the gambit drag on without a plan.

examples.caption: White to move (move 9). White gave up the c-pawn in the Queen's Gambit and Black grabbed it. Now 9.Bxc4 wins it back and develops the bishop in one move. It is the strongest move and White is slightly better: the recapture is good because it fits White's development.
examples.source: Firouzja vs Praggnanandhaa, Norway Chess 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2024-open/round-6/Whq5YPU7/mUVCSFEb)

items.title: Answer a4 with b4 to claim space (in some structures)
items.text: When your opponent tries to disturb you on the wing with a4, you can answer with b4 to claim space, take squares from the knights and strengthen the structure.
items.check: Softened: this is right in some structures, not in all. Check what b4 leaves behind (the c4 square and the pawn on a-file).

examples.caption: White to move (move 14). Black has just pushed ...a4. White answers at once with 14.b4, challenging the pawn and claiming queenside space. White is slightly better. (Black later won the game, but the move itself is the strongest.)
examples.source: Wei, Yi vs Sindarov, Javokhir, FIDE Candidates Tournament 2026, 2026 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-candidates-2026-open/round-6/WmbQrSNz/lkyNaDkn)

examples.caption: White to move (move 9). Mirror case: Black has pushed ...a5 and White meets it with 9.b4, grabbing space on the wing. White is slightly better, and this is the strongest move. White went on to win this game.
examples.source: Firouzja, Alireza vs Keymer, Vincent, 2026 Norway Chess Open, 2026 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2026-open/round-5-armageddon/JQI4Qhk5/83EDDlTP)

items.title: Scandinavian: queenside pressure against slow development
items.text: If White delays developing the minor pieces in the Scandinavian, play on the queenside with quick pawn pressure to surprise them.
items.check: Draft: this is a specific idea that I could not confirm in a concrete line. It needs an example position from Peter before it gets a page.

items.title: Avoid tricks and gambits as your main plan
items.text: Quick opening tricks (such as the Schiller Gambit or early queen attacks) look fun for a fast win, but in the long run they give bad positions, a lead in development for your opponent and a weak pawn structure.
items.check: Checked: sound as a long-term strategy. This does not contradict our trap lessons: they teach you to recognize traps and not fall for them, not to rely on them.

examples.caption: White to move (move 5). White went for a quick attack on f7 with Qh5 and Bc4. Black answered with ...Nc6, ...g6 (hitting the queen) and ...Nf6, blocking the f-file, so White has only a bishop and a queen out. Black is slightly better, even with White's best play.

items.title: Do not push pawns aimlessly
items.text: Do not shove pawns around in the opening unless it helps control the centre or develop your minor pieces.
items.check: Checked: standard.

examples.caption: White to move (move 6). Four of White's five moves were flank pawn moves (a3, h3, g3, b3). Black meanwhile took the centre with ...d5 and ...e5 and developed both knights and a bishop. Black is clearly better.

items.title: Finish development before you attack
items.text: Do not attack too early (with premature bishop or pawn moves) when your position is not fully developed. Incomplete development leaves holes your opponent can punish tactically.
items.check: Checked: standard. The exception is a concrete attack you have calculated. Also covers: do not go looking for complications or early flank pawn pushes before your own pieces are safe.

examples.caption: White to move (move 10). Black's last move ...b5 tried to chase the bishop, but the knight on b8, the bishop on f8 and the rook on h8 are still undeveloped and the king is in the centre. 10.Nxb5! is the strongest move, and White is winning.
examples.source: Morphy vs Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard, Paris 1858 ("Opera Game"; moves from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opera_Game)

items.title: Trade only when it gains something
items.text: Do not make pointless trades in the centre or the opening. If a trade gives you nothing tangible but helps the opponent develop their pieces (such as a queen or knight) with tempo, avoid it. Every trade needs a tactical or positional purpose.
items.check: Checked. Softened: a trade is fine when it removes a strong enemy piece or fixes a structure in your favour. Also covers: never trade pawns or pieces automatically. Ask: "Does this help my opponent build a strong pawn chain or develop for free?" Also covers: keep the tension. Do not capture in the centre or on the wing if it helps the opponent post a knight or pawn on a better square. Release the tension only when it confuses the opponent or activates your pieces, not just to resolve it. Also covers: before you trade, ask whether you are activating the opponent's pieces or removing one of their weaknesses.

examples.caption: White to move (move 8). White trades 8.Bxd7+ Qxd7. The trade has no purpose except to bring Black's queen out, and after 9.Ne5 Qd4 Black hits two pieces with tempo. The most accurate move was 8.a3, with White slightly better; after the trade Black is slightly better. A punished violation.
examples.source: Keymer, Vincent vs Praggnanandhaa R, 2026 Norway Chess Open, 2026 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2026-open/round-4-armageddon/xux5E5V6/nxCTIeLm)

items.title: Choose the active square over the default routine
items.text: Do not choose a square out of habit. Ask which square creates the most concrete pressure. A fianchetto is often right; sometimes Bd3 or Be2 is better.
items.check: Checked. Softened: the standard squares are standard for a reason, so the exception needs a concrete reason in the position.

examples.caption: White to move (move 8). White does not need a fianchetto or Be2: the bishop belongs on d3, aiming at the kingside and supporting e4. White is slightly better, and Bd3 is nearly as good as Bh4. Ask which square creates real pressure, not which is the habit.
examples.source: Sindarov, Javokhir vs Praggnanandhaa R, Tata Steel Chess Masters, 2026 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-chess-2026-masters/round-12/ELcnJ2BR/niWOOj1I)

items.title: Develop quickly: time matters
items.text: Bring your pieces into the game quickly and directly. Do not waste precious time on distractions or aimless moves; focus on fast, efficient development, so you can outnumber the opponent later on.
items.check: Checked. Same idea as: finish development before you attack, and be economical with your moves.

examples.caption: White to move (move 12). White develops the rook with a threat: 12.O-O-O. Black's bishop on f8 and rook on h8 are still at home. It is the strongest move, White is winning, and Rxd7 is threatened.
examples.source: Morphy vs Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard, Paris 1858 ("Opera Game"; moves from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opera_Game)

items.title: Build a system opening
items.text: Use a fixed set-up that lets you play the same solid plan against almost any reply, so you have less theory to remember.
items.check: Checked: a real approach (the Colle, London or similar systems). The label 'peer-to-peer recognition' in the notes looks like a dictation error, so I used 'system opening'. The price is less flexibility against well-prepared opponents. This works for Black too: a repeating Black set-up against almost any White move means little theory to remember.

examples.caption: White to move (move 8). White has played the London set-up: Bf4 (now g3), e3, c3, Bd3, and finishes with Nbd2. The same plan works against many Black set-ups. The position is about equal, and this is nearly the strongest move. White won this game.
examples.source: Caruana, Fabiano vs Van Foreest, Jorden, Tata Steel Chess Tournament 2025 Masters, 2025 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-chess-2025-masters/round-2/LPs7X3dM/HO7lkq69)

items.title: Use a flexible knight move to prepare e4
items.text: Nd2 instead of Nc3 keeps the c-pawn free and prepares e4, a break your opponent usually has to take into account.
items.check: Checked for d4 + e3 set-ups. Softened: it does not force one reply, but ...d5 is the natural one.

examples.caption: White to move (move 11). The knight went to d2 (not c3), and with Nf3 it backs up the e4 break. 11.e4 hits the d5 pawn and takes space in the centre; it is also the strongest move, and White is slightly better.
examples.source: Keymer vs Gukesh, Norway Chess 2026 Open (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2026-open/round-6/Hs6Gw8p0/mJyld5aw)

items.title: Support your centre pawn, then challenge
items.text: Support your centre pawn with a pawn and a piece, then build up with c4.
items.check: Wording in the source was unclear (which pawn is doubly defended). Kept as a draft until we confirm the position with Peter.

items.title: Queen to b3 at the right moment
items.text: Qb3 can work when b7 is hard to defend and the queen cannot be driven away with tempo. Check that first: ...Na5, ...Nb4 or ...Bf5 can hit the queen.
items.check: Checked: a known idea. Softened: only when b7 is really loose and the queen cannot be harassed (for example by ...Nxd4 or ...Qb6 tricks). The queen-out-too-early rule still applies.

examples.caption: White to move (move 7). Qb3 hits b7. Before playing it, check for tempo hits: ...Nb4 is covered by c3 and the bishop is on g4, not f5. 7.Qb3 is the strongest move and the position is about equal; Black answered ...Qc8 to defend the pawn.
examples.source: Firouzja vs Ding Liren, Norway Chess 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2024-open/round-4/4JSenCaJ/iZ0cIhtU)

items.title: Hunt the defending bishop
items.text: If your opponent puts a bishop on f5 or g4 to stop your e4 break, force a trade or chase it with a knight move to h4 to weaken their defence.
items.check: Checked: a typical plan in e3 set-ups. Check that your knight on h4 is not trapped.

examples.caption: White to move (move 5). Black's bishop on f5 stops White's e4 break. 5.Nh4 attacks it, so the bishop must move away or be traded. Nh4 is the strongest move and the position is about equal; in the game Black retreated ...Bd7.
examples.source: Caruana vs Duda, Sinquefield Cup 2025 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/gct-sinquefield-cup-2025-sinquefield-cup/round-1/LcjP5YKp/9kZcwDRI)

items.title: Bring the queen to the centre
items.text: Once the enemy bishop is off the diagonal, you can move the queen (often after a trade) to the centre to control e4 and raise the pressure.
items.check: Checked: sound. Do not leave the queen loose.

examples.caption: White to move (move 8). Black has traded the light-squared bishop for White's Bd3, so that diagonal is clear. Recapturing with the queen, Qxd3, brings it to a central square where it eyes e4 and keeps the position flexible. Qxd3 is clearly the strongest move.
examples.source: Nguyen, Ngoc Truong Son vs Tabatabaei, M. Amin, 45th Chess Olympiad, Budapest, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/45th-chess-olympiad-budapest-2024-open-i/round-7/CphdUotb/RszxMOuc)

items.title: Punish a forced short castle
items.text: If your opponent has to castle short while your pieces and pawns already point at the kingside, destructive sacrifices can be waiting, such as a bishop sacrifice on h6.
items.check: Draft: the classic sacrifice is Bxh7+ (the Greek gift). I could not confirm Bxh6 as a standard idea. Needs a concrete position and a calculation before publishing.

items.title: Punish passive play with a direct break
items.text: Against passive play, prepare and then open the centre with e4 when your pieces are ready.
items.check: Checked: sound. Make sure the break is prepared. Another lesson says the same: if the opponent answers passively (slow bishop or pawn moves), open the centre at once, for example with d4.

examples.caption: White to move (move 16). Black has played quietly: pawns on b6, d6, e6 and a cramped bishop on b7. White's pieces are ready with Re1, Nd2 and Bg3, so e4 now seizes the centre and gains space. e4 is the strongest move, slightly more accurate than the alternatives.
examples.source: Olsen, Filip Boe vs Jones, Gawain C B, 45th Chess Olympiad, Budapest, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/45th-chess-olympiad-budapest-2024-open-i/round-3/5tLXKIAf/TQ7OYRNu)

items.title: Create deadly forks in the middlegame
items.text: Keep a sharp eye for tactical moments where a centralized knight or an active queen attacks a king position and pieces at the same time.
items.check: Checked: forks are a main tactic. Use CCTO to find them.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 24). White's king on g1 is boxed in by its own pawns, and Black's knight on d4 is well centralised. Nf3+ forks the king, the queen on d1 and the rook on e1. Qxf3 loses to ...gxf3, so White must move the king and Black wins the exchange and is clearly better.
examples.source: Praggnanandhaa R vs Caruana, Fabiano, FIDE Candidates, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-candidates-2024-open/round-13/Dc0DQMaQ/jfTiqtRa)

items.title: Keep looking at 'poisoned' pawns
items.text: If your opponent leaves a pawn undefended or open to capture, check whether it is poisoned by a pin or a mate threat before you take it. Punish them with the material loss if it is.
items.check: Checked: always check before taking a free pawn (the same idea as the Fishing Pole Trap).

examples.caption: Black to move (move 9). The b2 pawn looks poisoned: Rb1 and Bb5 may trap the queen. Black checks and finds 9...Qxb2 10.Rb1 Qa3 11.Bb5 Nxd4, escaping. Taking is the strongest move, leaving White only slightly better; other moves leave White clearly better. The exception: a poisoned-looking pawn is fine once the lines are checked.
examples.source: Vachier-Lagrave, Maxime vs Aronian, Levon, Sinquefield Cup, 2025 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/gct-sinquefield-cup-2025-sinquefield-cup/round-3/tEgitHjc/ZMmneBfO)

items.title: Choose a reliable, repeatable system: the Italian Game
items.text: Play an opening such as the Italian Game (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4), which suits every level from beginner to grandmaster. You play on flexible plans and development patterns instead of memorizing endless variations.
items.check: Checked: the Italian is played at every level. Some lines are sharp and full of theory (Evans Gambit, Two Knights). The slow plan-based lines (Giuoco Pianissimo) are the ones that fit this principle.

examples.caption: White to move (move 4). In game 2 of the 2024 World Championship, White chooses the quiet Italian with 4.d3. Plans are simple: castle, c3 or Nc3, and a slow build-up. The position is about equal, and this is the strongest move. Even at the top level the plan matters more than memorised lines.
examples.source: Ding, Liren vs Gukesh D, FIDE World Championship Match 2024, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-world-championship-2024/game-2/YL0LEwAL/AljZUNDm)

items.title: A knight plan in the Italian Game
items.text: Use the knight manoeuvre Nbd2-f1-g3 in slow Italian set-ups. Bring the c1 bishop out when it has a useful square, often e3 or g5.
items.check: Checked: a typical plan in the slow Italian (c3, d3, Nbd2-f1-g3).

examples.caption: White to move (move 8). The knight has already travelled from d2 to f1 in this slow Italian set-up. Now Ng3 completes the manoeuvre, putting it on a useful kingside square where it eyes f5 and h5. The c1 bishop can come out later, for example to g5. Ng3 is almost the strongest move.
examples.source: Caruana, Fabiano vs Firouzja, Alireza, Norway Chess, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2024-open/round-7/4FLBpAW3/gPXBZQj3)

items.title: A simple, universal Black system against 1.d4
items.text: As Black, pick a reliable set-up (such as the Queen's Gambit Declined with ...Nf6 and ...e6/...d5) that you can use against almost any White move, so you do not have to learn thousands of variations.
items.check: Checked: the QGD is a classic system. No system covers everything (the London and Catalan need their own plans), but the core stays the same.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 3). Black has Nf6 and e6 on the board, and ...d5 completes the Queen's Gambit Declined set-up. The same plan works whatever move order White picks (Nf3, Nc3 or g3). ...d5 is the strongest move, with White only slightly better.
examples.source: Ding, Liren vs Carlsen, Magnus, Norway Chess, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2024-open/round-1/I9TLGEOt/NKrhl0d7)

items.title: Develop the kingside first, then castle
items.text: In this set-up develop your kingside minor pieces (knight and bishop) first and get your king safe with short castling in time.
items.check: Checked: standard.

examples.caption: White to move (move 5). Knight on f3, bishop on c4, d3 played: the kingside minor pieces are out. Now 5.O-O brings the king to safety. White is slightly better, and this is among the strongest moves. Develop first, then castle.
examples.source: Gukesh D vs Wei, Yi, Tata Steel Chess Tournament 2025 Masters, 2025 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-chess-2025-masters/round-11/iAu6JSH1/Dfxt7E7j)

items.title: Challenge the centre from the flank (...c5)
items.text: Support your position with flexible pawn structures (such as ...b6, ...Bb7 and the break ...c5) to raise the pressure on White's centre and open lines.
items.check: Checked: a typical plan in Queen's Indian and Benoni-type structures.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 6). Black has set up with ...b6 and ...Bb7, and the bishop now eyes the long diagonal. The flank pawn break ...c5 hits White's d4 pawn and starts to open lines against the centre. ...c5 is nearly as accurate as ...Be7.
examples.source: Warmerdam, Max vs Ding, Liren, Tata Steel Masters, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-masters-2024/round-12/EDCwDiqA/KqzR35Wf)

items.title: Choose the Sicilian Defence for a dynamic position
items.text: With 1...c5 Black fights for the centre indirectly, stops White from setting up two central pawns side by side, and creates an asymmetric, aggressive game.
items.check: Checked: that is the idea of the Sicilian. The main lines are full of theory, so it suits players who enjoy learning it.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 5). After 1...c5 Black traded the c-pawn for White's d-pawn, giving an uneven structure. 5...a6 (the Najdorf) is the strongest move, with White only slightly better. Black keeps many plans, such as ...e5 or ...g6, and won this game.
examples.source: Esipenko, Andrey vs Caruana, Fabiano, FIDE Candidates Tournament 2026, 2026 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-candidates-2026-open/round-14/oBkeHnpi/gi2VX6NQ)

items.title: Play the flexible ...e6 against side lines
items.text: Against early side lines such as Bc4, ...e6 is a very solid, low-theory set-up for Black.
items.check: Softened: low-theory against sidelines. In the main Open Sicilian there is a lot of theory.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 4). White has gone for a quiet, low-theory Bc4 and d3 set-up against the Sicilian. Black answers with the solid ...e6, which opens the f8 bishop, prepares castling and needs no memorised lines. ...e6 is the strongest move, and the alternatives are nearly as good.
examples.source: Haring, Filip vs Gurel, Ediz, 45th Chess Olympiad, Budapest, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/45th-chess-olympiad-budapest-2024-open-i/round-3/5tLXKIAf/qQbGvqcd)

items.title: Hit the centre with ...d5 when White is inaccurate
items.text: When White plays suboptimal bishop or pawn moves, answer at once with ...d5 to open the centre and chase the enemy bishop.
items.check: Checked: a standard reaction, as long as your pieces are developed enough to support it.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 4). White has castled and left the e4 pawn and the c4 bishop without any central support. Black strikes at once with ...d5, hitting the bishop and opening the centre while White's pieces are not ready. ...d5 is the strongest move, and the position is roughly equal.
examples.source: Van Foreest, Jorden vs Praggnanandhaa R, Tata Steel Masters, 2022 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-masters-2022/round-3/Le9ZUpD5/RyOJdEh4)

items.title: Develop by the basic principles, even in a sharp opening
items.text: Even in a sharp opening like the Sicilian the fundamentals apply: develop your minor pieces, control the centre and get your king safe in time (often with short castling).
items.check: Checked: standard.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 11). Even in a sharp Sicilian, Black has developed Nf6, Nc5 and Be7, controls the centre with ...e5, and now castles. 11...O-O is among the strongest moves, and the position is about equal. Black went on to win this game.
examples.source: Caruana, Fabiano vs Nakamura, Hikaru, Norway Chess, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2024-open/round-1/I9TLGEOt/hkSR1sG5)

items.title: Use the half-open c-file and the queen on c7
items.text: The queen on c7 is thematic in the Open Sicilian: it eyes the c-file and supports ...b5 and ...a6 expansion. Watch for Nb5 and Nd5 tricks.
items.check: Checked: typical for several Sicilian set-ups.

examples.caption: White to move (move 13). Black's queen on c7 is on the half-open c-file, which also makes it a target. Nd5 attacks it with tempo and the queen has to retreat. Nd5 is clearly the best move here: the quiet alternatives leave White slightly worse.
examples.source: Caruana, Fabiano vs Volokitin, Andrei, 45th Chess Olympiad, Budapest, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/45th-chess-olympiad-budapest-2024-open-i/round-4/6wJduA1I/cAgoSdmC)

items.title: Neutralize early queen attacks with simplicity
items.text: Early queen tricks against the Sicilian (such as Qh5 or Qf3) are easily parried with ...e6. The exposed queen can then lose time to your developing knights.
items.check: Checked: ...e6 is the standard calm answer. These tricks are rare, but good to know.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 11). White brought the queen out early (Qd3, now Qe3). Black simply developed: ...g6, ...Bg7, ...O-O, ...Nc6, ...Be6, and the queen has lost time. 11...Rc8 is the strongest move, and the position is about equal. Not the ...e6 trick itself, but the same idea.
examples.source: Esipenko, Andrey vs Caruana, Fabiano, FIDE Candidates Tournament 2026, 2026 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-candidates-2026-open/round-14/oBkeHnpi/gi2VX6NQ)

items.title: Be careful with an early ...e5 in the Sicilian
items.text: In the early opening ...e5 leaves a hole on d5 that White's pieces control. Check before you play it.
items.check: Corrected: "almost never" was too strong. Some lines (such as the Sveshnikov and Kalashnikov) accept the d5 hole on purpose in return for activity.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 5). 5...e5 leaves a hole on d5 that White's knights can use (Bb5+, Nf5). White is a bit better after it, slightly more than after 5...a6. A small price Black accepted knowingly, and an exception to the rule of caution. Black won.
examples.source: Caruana, Fabiano vs Nakamura, Hikaru, Norway Chess, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2024-open/round-1/I9TLGEOt/hkSR1sG5)

items.title: Answer an early bishop pin with ...h6
items.text: When a bishop pins your knight on f6 (or f3) early with Bg5 (or Bg4), ask the question at once with ...h6. If the bishop stays on the pin, you can break it with ...g5.
items.check: Checked: standard. Softened: ...g5 weakens your own king, so play it only if the centre is stable and the tactics work (see the centre principle below).

examples.caption: Black to move (move 5). White's bishop on g5 pins the f6 knight. Black asks the bishop a question at once with ...h6, so it must decide whether to retreat or to keep the pin. ...h6 is also the strongest move here. Later ...g5 can break the pin if the bishop stays.
examples.source: Gukesh D vs Suleymanli, Aydin, 45th Chess Olympiad, Budapest, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/45th-chess-olympiad-budapest-2024-open-i/round-5/IXM4hVtE/PRu4qZt7)

items.title: Lock the bishop in and switch to the other wing
items.text: If after ...g5 the bishop is driven back to a passive corner such as g3, where your pawns and its own pawns block it, it is out of play. Block that side and move the initiative to the other wing, where you have more pieces.
items.check: Softened: "playing with an extra piece" is a figure of speech. A buried bishop is a big positional asset, not a material one. Check that it cannot break out with a pawn move.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 16). ...g5 drove the bishop to g3. Now 16...h4 hits it again, and after Bh2 the bishop sits behind its own pawns on d4 and e3. White is slightly better, and 16...h4 is practically the strongest move. Black can then play on the queenside.
examples.source: Gukesh D vs Caruana, Fabiano, Tata Steel Chess Tournament 2025 Masters, 2025 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-chess-2025-masters/round-3/rVxHrSCY/QLnlh22p)

items.title: Strengthen the centre before the flank can exploit the pin
items.text: Before the opponent profits on the wing from the pin, strengthen the centre with flexible moves such as ...c5 or ...e5, so they have no counterplay there. Centre control neutralizes a flank attack on a pinned piece.
items.check: Checked.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 5). White's bishop on g5 pins the f6 knight, and many players would reply ...h6 automatically. Here Black hits the centre with ...c5 instead, so a flank attack on the pin gets little counterplay. ...c5 is the strongest move, slightly more accurate than ...h6 or ...d5.
examples.source: Shevchenko, Kirill vs So, Wesley, 45th Chess Olympiad, Budapest, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/45th-chess-olympiad-budapest-2024-open-i/round-6/se59qqeE/1DHGmcbp)

items.title: Reposition a knight to chase the bishop (Nf1-e3)
items.text: If the opponent keeps the bishop and you want to increase the pressure, use a classic knight route (such as via f1 to e3) to chase it away actively and regroup harmoniously, without weakening your pawn structure.
items.check: Checked: context-dependent, it works when e3 is not under attack by a pawn.

examples.caption: White to move (move 16). Black's bishop on g4 pins the f3 knight to the queen. White's knight has come round to f1, and Ne3 now attacks the bishop and keeps the pawn structure intact. Ne3 is the strongest move, slightly more accurate than Bb3.
examples.source: Firouzja, Alireza vs Abdusattorov, Nodirbek, Tata Steel Masters, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-masters-2024/round-4/msGCthzJ/MYMAZaQX)

items.title: Pick a middlegame plan
items.text: After the opening, choose one clear aim, such as a specific pawn break. A plan gives direction to every following move and puts the opponent under pressure.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 18). Black picks one clear aim: the pawn break ...b4, hitting White's a3 pawn and opening the queenside, instead of shuffling pieces. After 18...b4 axb4 cxb4 Black has a passed-looking b-pawn and play there. It is slightly less accurate than Nd5.
examples.source: Aravindh, Chithambaram VR. vs Niemann, Hans Moke, Tata Steel Chess Masters, 2026 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-chess-2026-masters/round-4/TU7qC17C/Ay87teqm)

items.title: Prepare the break, then play it
items.text: Play a thematic pawn break once your pieces stand well to support it. Breaking too early loses pawns; patient preparation slowly squeezes the opponent.
items.check: Checked: a good rule of thumb, not an absolute one. With the initiative, an early break can be right.

examples.caption: White to move (move 9). White has finished development first: Bd3, Nbd2, Nf3 and Re1 all stand behind the e3 pawn, and the king is castled. Only now does e4 come, opening the centre with every piece ready. e4 is clearly the best move here, more accurate than the quiet alternatives.
examples.source: Wei, Yi vs Vidit, Santosh Gujrathi, Tata Steel Masters, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-masters-2024/round-13/MIewWyMv/HaB0gcHA)

items.title: Block the line instead of adding a defender
items.text: A pawn under attack does not always need another defender. Sometimes you can cut the attacking line. That keeps your pieces active instead of passive.

examples.caption: White to move (move 16). Black's queen on e5 attacks the undefended b2 pawn along the long diagonal. Instead of passively defending it, White plays Bc3, putting a piece on the line and hitting the queen at the same time. Bc3 is the strongest move; the natural alternatives O-O or Be3 allow ...Qxb2 and are somewhat worse.
examples.source: Bachmann, Axel vs Vachier-Lagrave, Maxime, 45th Chess Olympiad, Budapest, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/45th-chess-olympiad-budapest-2024-open-i/round-2/o2ts84YP/OYtMTcWI)

examples.caption: White to move (move 15). Black's queen on d4 eyes the b2 pawn. Rather than guarding it, White blocks the diagonal with Nc3, which also brings the b1 knight into play. Nc3 is the strongest move, slightly more accurate than Rd1 or Re2.
examples.source: Nakamura, Hikaru vs Caruana, Fabiano, Norway Chess, 2025 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2025-open/round-6/4MpGqf5j/hlM8nPbU)

items.title: Simple, controlled play wins
items.text: Simple, controlled play wins many games at club level. Avoid unsound sacrifices and convert small advantages.
items.check: Checked: sound for club play. One pawn is enough only if you convert carefully.

examples.caption: White to move (move 32) with a clear edge and equal material. No sacrifice is needed. 32.Qxb7 Rxb7 trades queens, removes Black's counterplay and keeps the better position. Calm exchanges like this convert small advantages; it is the strongest move.
examples.source: Giri, Anish vs Praggnanandhaa R, Tata Steel Chess Tournament 2025 Masters, 2025 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-chess-2025-masters/round-9/y1UCH4bb/Z0Qi1OnD)

items.title: Optimize: improve your worst piece
items.text: When there is no check, capture or forcing threat, improve your passive pieces, starting with the ones still on your back rank (minor pieces first).
items.check: Checked: this is the 'improve your worst piece' rule. For example by bringing a rook to an open or semi-open file. Do it systematically: find your least active piece (a passive rook or bishop) and bring it to an active (semi-)open file. Same idea as the least active piece: look at the piece that does the least or is stuck, and fix that first. Do not attack aimlessly; improve the weakest spot in your own army.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 15). Nothing is forcing here, and the bishop on f8 is the last minor piece still at home. 15...Bd6 puts it on its best diagonal and challenges White's bishop on f4. It is the strongest move, and the position is about equal.
examples.source: Jorden van Foreest vs Viswanathan Anand, Tata Steel, Wijk aan Zee 2019 (https://www.pgnmentor.com/players/Anand.zip)

items.title: Improve with a purpose
items.text: When you reposition a piece such as your queen, prefer an active square that attacks a target (an undefended piece or a pawn) over a passive retreat.
items.check: Checked: sound. Do not leave a piece hanging for the sake of an active square. Also covers: improve all your pieces to their best squares, even with quiet waiting moves, before you start risky actions. Do not attack early or force complications while you have a weakness in your own position. Patient improvement reduces blunders and builds pressure.

examples.caption: White to move (move 23). Black's knight on c4 is undefended. 23.Qe2 puts the queen on an active square that attacks it, and the knight is lost in the main line. White is winning; quieter queen moves such as Qh5 or Qb3 leave White worse.
examples.source: Vladimir Kramnik vs Anatoly Karpov, Siemens Giants, Frankfurt 1999 (https://www.pgnmentor.com/players/Kramnik.zip)

items.title: Attack the backward pawn
items.text: A pawn that cannot be supported by other pawns and cannot advance is a weakness. Pile your pressure on it and try to win it step by step.
items.check: Corrected: it is a target, not literally a 'dead pawn'. You will not always win it, but it ties down your opponent's pieces.

examples.caption: White to move (move 29). Black's d5 pawn is backward: the c-pawn has run ahead to c4, there is no e-pawn, and White's e3 pawn controls d4. 29.Rd1 adds a rook to the knight already eyeing d5. White is clearly better, while the next best move leaves White slightly worse, and the pawn falls in the main line.
examples.source: Yasser Seirawan vs Boris Spassky, Niksic 1983 (https://www.pgnmentor.com/players/Spassky.zip)

items.title: Build up pressure, then break
items.text: When your opponent's pieces are all tied to defending one weakness, create the breaking move (such as an advancing pawn) to open the position. The defence often cracks.
items.check: Softened: 'often cracks', not always.

examples.caption: White to move (move 17). White has prepared with a4, b4 and Rb1 against Black's queenside, where the king and queen stand. Only then comes the break 17.b5, opening the a- and b-files towards them. Build up first, then open the position; it is the strongest move, and White is clearly better.
examples.source: Abdusattorov, Nodirbek vs Mendonca, Leon Luke, Tata Steel Chess Tournament 2025 Masters, 2025 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-chess-2025-masters/round-2/LPs7X3dM/bGZYTbtZ)

items.title: Pawns leave holes behind
items.text: A pawn that moves forward can never protect the square it left. When pawns advance too far, holes appear where the opponent can plant a piece for good.
items.check: Checked: true. Softened: a hole only hurts if an enemy piece can actually use it.

examples.caption: White to move (move 18). Black has no c-pawn and no e-pawn left, so no pawn can ever attack d5. 18.Nd5 plants a knight there for good, and f6 is soon lost to the knight and the b2 bishop. White is winning, and the next best move would give only about equal.
examples.source: Vasily Smyslov vs Jan Timman, Moscow 1981 (https://www.pgnmentor.com/players/Smyslov.zip)

items.title: Prophylaxis: control the key squares
items.text: Cut off the opponent's counterplay by controlling the key invasion squares before they get there. A key square held in advance leaves them with nothing to do.
items.check: Checked: a classic idea (prophylaxis). It does not make the opponent helpless. Ask yourself every move: which checks, captures or threats can my opponent play? If needed, play a prophylactic move before it gets painful.

examples.caption: White to move (move 9). Nothing is attacked, but Black's bishop and knight both want g4 (...Bg4 pins the f3-knight). 9.h3 takes that square away before Black can use it. A quiet move that removes the opponent's best idea; it is the strongest move, and the position is about equal.
examples.source: Jan-Krzysztof Duda vs Fabiano Caruana, Round 10: Jan-Krzysztof Duda - Fabiano Caruana, 2022 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-candidates-tournament-2022/round-10/FWJYzJJJ/CDGcSv2h)

items.title: After you win material, check their compensation
items.text: Ask what the opponent got in return, for example the bishop pair. Then trade off that specific advantage.
items.check: Checked: good habit. Material is not everything, so look at what the other side gained.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 22). Black is a pawn up; White's compensation is the two bishops. 22...Nbxd3 trades a knight for one of them, and after cxd3 Nxd3 Black also wins a second pawn. Ask what the opponent got in return, then trade that exact asset. It is the strongest move, and Black is much better.
examples.source: Van Foreest, Jorden vs Gukesh, D, Tata Steel Masters 2024, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-masters-2024/round-6/ubgeWaHz/hRafgim5)

items.title: Optimize with a pawn move (gain space)
items.text: A pawn move can also be an improving move, if it seriously restricts the opponent's pieces or takes extra space, for example ...c6 against the opponent's pieces.
items.check: Checked: a good idea. Check the weaknesses the pawn move leaves behind.

examples.caption: White to move (move 12). No piece needs improving more than the pawn on g4: 12.g5 kicks the f6-knight away from its good square and grabs kingside space, so Black's pieces get fewer squares. A pawn move that restricts is a real improving move; it is the strongest move, and White is slightly better.
examples.source: Ian Nepomniachtchi vs Alireza Firouzja, Round 4: Ian Nepomniachtchi - Alireza Firouzja, 2022 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-candidates-tournament-2022/round-4/0QuWnLkU/g1rO1xmS)

items.title: Activate a passive piece in time
items.text: If one of your pieces, such as a rook, has stood passively on the back rank through the whole middlegame, look for a moment to activate it for a break or to pressure the enemy weaknesses.
items.check: Checked: this is the "improve your worst piece" idea for the rook. See also: the least active piece principle. Also covers: keep all pieces active, scan regularly for a sleeping piece and move it to an open file or a better post first.

examples.caption: White to move (move 20). White's a1 rook has not moved all game. 20.Rad1 brings it into play on the d-file, behind the d4 pawn. In the game Black traded on e5 and the file opened. Rad1 is the strongest move and leaves White much better, while the next best move gives a smaller, clear edge.
examples.source: Magnus Carlsen vs Dambasuren Batsuren, 44th Olympiad, Chennai 2022 (https://www.pgnmentor.com/players/Carlsen.zip)

items.title: Create a weak pawn in the enemy camp
items.text: Trade pieces or open lines in a way that leaves your opponent with a weak, backward or isolated pawn, then keep permanent pressure on it.
items.check: Checked: the way to get the target in the first place. See "Attack the backward pawn".

examples.caption: Black to move (move 7). 7...Bxc3 8.bxc3 leaves White with doubled c-pawns on c3 and c4, a lasting weakness in the pawn structure. Bxc3 is Black's strongest move, and the position is about equal; the other tries leave White clearly better.
examples.source: Maxime Vachier-Lagrave vs Fabiano Caruana, Grenke Chess Classic, Baden-Baden 2018 (https://www.pgnmentor.com/players/Caruana.zip)

items.title: Read the pawn structure as a skeleton
items.text: Read the structure to see which squares and routes are ideal for your pieces, such as a knight route to f4.
items.check: Checked: pawn structure decides where your pieces belong.

examples.caption: White to move (move 23). Read the pawns: no black pawn can ever attack d5 (the c-pawn has gone to b5 and the e-pawn is already past it), and White's e4 pawn supports it. So d5 is a permanent hole and the ideal square for the c3-knight. 23.Nd5 is clearly the strongest move, and White is clearly better.
examples.source: Praggnanandhaa R vs Carlsen, Magnus, Norway Chess, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2024-open/round-3/xmZcMs9U/Rq9e5H7u)

items.title: Park the queen behind your pieces (a8 or b7)
items.text: In some closed structures the queen can go to secondary squares such as a8 behind your own pieces, where it builds a battery on a diagonal or file without being exposed to a trade.
items.check: Checked: a real idea (for example ...Qa8 behind a bishop on b7 in some Queen's Indian lines). Only in specific structures.

examples.caption: White to move (move 15), Gukesh vs Ding. The long diagonal is lined up: the bishop on c3 aims at f6. 15.Qb2 puts the queen behind the bishop on the same diagonal, a battery with a secondary square for the queen. Playable, slightly less accurate than the best move; mirror of the Qa8 idea.
examples.source: Gukesh D vs Ding, Liren, FIDE World Championship Match 2024, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-world-championship-2024/game-9/HMJKeeue/mp31I4cA)

items.title: Keep control of the break squares (e5, c5)
items.text: In open or semi-open positions, use your active pieces to stop your opponent from making space-gaining breaks in the centre, such as ...e5 or ...c5.
items.check: Checked: this is prophylaxis against breaks.

examples.caption: White to move (move 15). Black wants the break ...e5. 15.Rc5 adds a rook to the bishop on d4 so that e5 stays well covered (as accurate as the best move, with the position about equal). In the game Black pushed ...e5 anyway and after 16.Nc4 stood clearly worse. The break fails while you control the square.
examples.source: Firouzja, Alireza vs Abasov, Nijat, FIDE Candidates 2024, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-candidates-2024-open/round-11/46ohJ8Qt/yALfu63F)

items.title: Check that your pieces do not get in each other's way
items.text: The higher you climb, the less standard development is enough. Calculate that your pieces do not block each other and that you do not block flexible plans too early (such as a flank break with c4 or d4).
items.check: Checked: true. The wording in the source was general, so I kept it general.
items.scenario: Try this: before you play a developing move, look at the lines it blocks. A knight on d2 blocks the c1 bishop, a bishop on e2 can block the f1 rook's path to the centre, and a queen on d2 can block both rooks. If a piece blocks another, ask whether a different square (or a different order) lets both work.

items.title: Target weak pawns before risky king attacks
items.text: Instead of a reckless king attack, put steady pressure on the opponent's weak pawns with your pieces and rooks. This builds your advantage gradually without needless risk.
items.check: Softened: not either-or. A well-prepared king attack is fine; this is the lower-risk default.

examples.caption: White to move (move 16). Black's a5 pawn has no neighbouring pawn to protect it. No king attack is needed: 16.Nxa5 simply wins it, and the other moves are about equal. Steady pressure on a weak pawn builds the advantage safely. It is clearly the strongest move, and White is clearly better.
examples.source: Teimour Radjabov vs Hikaru Nakamura, Round 9: Teimour Radjabov - Hikaru Nakamura, 2022 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-candidates-tournament-2022/round-9/pk9gRSMB/zwRK3Eyj)

items.title: Use the centre to restrict your opponent
items.text: A strong presence in the centre, for example a knight on an outpost, takes away the room your opponent's bishops, knights and rooks need to move. Centre control is not only for your own development, but also to limit theirs.
items.check: Checked.

examples.caption: White to move (move 17). Black has no c- or e-pawn left behind d6, so no pawn can ever chase a knight from there. 17.Nd6 hits the rook on c8 and cramps Black's pieces, which must give way. Nd6 is the strongest move and leaves White slightly better, while the next move is only equal.
examples.source: Vasily Smyslov vs Wolfgang Uhlmann, Mar del Plata 1966 (https://www.pgnmentor.com/players/Smyslov.zip)

items.title: Avoid trades when you have a space advantage
items.text: When you have more space or hold the opponent in a bind, avoid needless trades: trades give the cramped side air and open lines for counterplay. Trade only if you get something out of it.
items.check: Contrast with: trade pieces when ahead in material. The difference is the type of advantage: with material up, simplify; with a space bind, keep pieces on.

examples.caption: White to move (move 32). White's pawns on c5, e5 and f5 give a clear space edge. 32.Bxd5 exd5 is a simple trade, but it frees Black's cramped position and removes the knight on d5. White keeps the tension with 32.Rc1 instead; it is more accurate, keeping White slightly better, while the trade leaves the position about equal.
examples.source: Carlsen, Magnus vs Caruana, Fabiano, Norway Chess 2025, 2025 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2025-open/round-9/Qv9cnRyb/JYYjPPaY)

items.title: Use space to switch your heavy pieces quickly
items.text: With more space you can move your rooks and queen easily from one wing to the other, while the opponent is stuck for room. Use that space as a transport route to concentrate on their weak spots.
items.check: Checked.

examples.caption: White to move (move 35). White's pawns on b5, g5 and h4 and the e3-f3 chain give extra room. 35.Rg4 swings the rook from the queenside to the kingside in one move along the free fourth rank, while Black's pieces are short of space. It is the strongest move, and White is much better.
examples.source: Magnus Carlsen vs Ian Nepomniachtchi, Sinquefield Cup, 2022 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/sinquefield-cup-grand-chess-tour-2022/round-1/w8G7sWaN/l5v1nDkY)

items.title: Drive knights back with pawns
items.text: Pawn advances that deny a knight its outposts can restrict it. Check that the advance does not weaken your own squares.
items.check: Softened: every pawn push leaves holes behind it (see pawns leave holes), so check which squares you give away.

examples.caption: White to move (move 16). Black's knight on e5 is well placed, so White kicks it with 16.f4. The knight must give up the centre (...Nc6 is expected). f4 leaves White much better, against only a clear edge for the next best move.
examples.source: Jose Raul Capablanca vs Frederick Yates, Barcelona 1929 (https://www.pgnmentor.com/players/Capablanca.zip)

items.title: Put rooks on open files
items.text: A rook is a linear piece that gains enormous power on an open or half-open file. Look for ways to manoeuvre your rooks to open files and dominate the edges and depth of the board.
items.check: Checked. If no file is open yet, prepare one with a pawn trade or break.

examples.caption: White to move (move 18). The d-file has no pawns of either colour. 18.Rad1 brings the rook from the back rank straight onto it and hits the queen on d7. It is the strongest move and leaves White clearly better; the next best move gives only a slight edge.
examples.source: Garry Kasparov vs Artur Yusupov, USSR Championship, Minsk 1979 (https://www.pgnmentor.com/players/Kasparov.zip)

items.title: Know the three kinds of weaknesses
items.text: There are three main weaknesses: weak colour complexes (diagonals not covered by your own bishops), weak squares or holes (often outposts for knights), and weak pawns (doubled, isolated and backward pawns). Fight each with the right piece.
items.check: Checked. Rule of thumb: colour complexes with bishops and queens, holes with knights, backward pawns with rooks and queens.

examples.caption: White to move (move 18). This is the colour-complex weakness: Black's only bishop is light-squared, so nothing guards the dark squares around his king. 18.Bg5 hits the queen on f6 from a dark square Black cannot contest and keeps the initiative. It is the strongest move, and White is much better.
examples.source: Wei, Yi vs Gukesh D, Norway Chess 2025, 2025 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2025-open/round-5-armageddon/b3lUTDzE/Ns5FeKTD)

items.title: Space is decided by your pawn chain
items.text: Space advantage is set by your pawn chain, the "mountain tops". The side with the most space controls the area behind its pawns and dictates where the action takes place. Play and attack on the part of the board where your pawn chain points and where you have the most space.
items.check: Softened: the opponent's counter is to attack the base of your chain. Space also needs good piece placement, or it becomes a target.

examples.caption: White to move (move 12). The chain d4-e5 (with b4 behind) is White's mountain top: everything behind it is White's room, and Black's pieces have few squares. White uses that freedom: 12.Nc5 plants a knight deep in Black's side and it is the strongest move, leaving White slightly better. The game was drawn.
examples.source: Caruana, Fabiano vs Praggnanandhaa R, FIDE Candidates 2024, 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-candidates-2024-open/round-7/X9LGGQoT/ChaqV75t)

items.title: Checks, captures, threats: a fixed thinking system
items.text: Run the same steps every move: Checks, Captures, Threats, then Optimize. It prevents blunders, stops you missing chances and gives consistently good moves. Use it for your opponent too: what checks, captures and threats can they play?
items.check: Checked: CCT is a standard method. The extra O (Optimize) is our coach's addition and is explained next under Middlegame plan.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 17). White just played Rc2, putting rook and king on the same knight-check square. Run the list: checks first. 17...Nd4+ forks king and rook and wins the exchange. Looking at checks before quiet moves found it at once.
examples.source: Keymer, Vincent vs Praggnanandhaa R, 2026 Norway Chess Open, 2026 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2026-open/round-4-armageddon/xux5E5V6/nxCTIeLm)

items.title: Beware a free piece when a rook pawn opens a file at your king
items.text: Do not just grab a 'free' piece when the opponent pushes a rook pawn to open a file towards your king. An offer like this opens attack lines, and your position can collapse in a few moves.
items.check: Example: in our Fishing Pole Trap (Ruy Lopez, Black sets it) the bait is a knight on g4 and Black opens the h-file against the castled king.

examples.caption: White to move after 5...h5 (the Fishing Pole line of the Ruy Lopez). Taking the 'free' knight with 6.hxg4? hxg4 opens the h-file at White's king and the evaluation swings from White being much better to Black winning. Calm moves such as 6.c3 or 6.d4 keep White clearly better.
examples.source: Ruy Lopez, Fishing Pole variation (opening theory)

items.title: Deal with infiltrators on your half
items.text: Do not leave enemy pieces on your side of the board alone. Trade or chase them early, otherwise they become the base for dangerous combinations against your king.
items.check: Softened: act on it quickly, but only when trading or chasing does not cost you more. Also covers: do not tolerate enemy outposts on your own half (first four ranks). Trade them off or drive them away before they become a nuisance. Softened: sometimes a trade costs you more than the outpost does, so check first. Also covers: neutralize an intruder before you start your own attack, so your half stays tidy and tactical blunders are less likely.

examples.caption: White to move (move 24). Black's knight has landed on e4, inside White's half. White does not leave it alone: 24.Nxe4 trades it off at once and the position stays level. This is the principle applied well.
examples.source: Ding Liren vs Gukesh D, FIDE World Championship Match 2024 Game 4 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-world-championship-2024/game-4/9DU8PRwg/5iq4Ivrk)

items.title: Back-rank safety
items.text: Watch for mate threats on the back rank, for you and for your opponent. Make a flight square (luft) for your king in time.
items.check: Also in the endgame: when you trade or sacrifice pieces, check the back rank first and adjust your defence in time.

examples.caption: White to move (move 30). Black's king on b8 has no luft: a7, b7 and c7 are all blocked by its own pawns. White sacrifices the queen with Qh8+; after Bxh8 comes Re8+ Qd8 Rxd8, mate. Make a flight square in time, and check your opponent's back rank too.

items.title: Master both kinds of blunders
items.text: Avoid giving away your own material (or walking into mate), and avoid missing the chances your opponent offers you. Both kinds of carelessness cost you the game.
items.check: Checked: both matter. One is a mistake you make, the other is a chance you miss.

examples.caption: White to move (move 29). Black grabbed a pawn with 28...dxc4 while his rook on f8 was already attacked by the bishop on g7. 29.Bxf8 wins the exchange (White is much better). Black gave material away by missing a threat; White took the chance.
examples.source: Caruana vs Erigaisi, Norway Chess 2025 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2025-open/round-3/BviKOlVd/EdGZbw91)

items.title: Look first, do not play too fast
items.text: Before you move, stop at every move of your opponent. Ask: what is the purpose of this move, what would he do with a free move, and does he have checks or captures? Only then choose your own move.
items.check: Checked: a good habit. It is the same question as "what does this move threaten?" Before carrying out your own plan, check what your opponent attacks and whether all your pieces are protected.

examples.caption: Black to move after 5.Nxe5 (Légal's trap). 5...Bxd1?? looks like winning a queen, but 6.Bxf7+ Ke7 7.Nd5# is mate. Checking the opponent's checks and captures first, as the principle says, finds the calm 5...dxe5. That is the strongest move.

items.title: Solve immediate problems first
items.text: When your opponent creates a threat, such as an attack on a piece or a mate threat, solving it comes before your own attack plan.
items.check: Checked: correct, with one exception: a stronger forcing move of your own (a check or a mate) can come first if you have calculated it.

examples.caption: White to move (move 8). Black's ...b5 attacks the bishop on a4. Tempting alternatives like 8.dxc5 or 8.f4 allow ...bxa4 and lose a piece. 8.Bb3 deals with the threat first and keeps a small edge.
examples.source: Carlsen vs Nakamura, Norway Chess 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2024-open/round-2/sbOHYOVj/3BmLduNX)

items.title: Set a trap with a defensive move
items.text: Sometimes a defensive or passive-looking move (such as moving a rook) is a clever trap. The opponent is punished when he tries to grab your poisoned pawn.
items.check: Checked: traps work well at club level. Only set one when your move is also fine if he does not fall for it. You can also offer a "poisoned" pawn: the opponent grabs it and ends up with badly placed pieces or an open file for your rooks (the poisoned-pawn idea is real, such as in the Najdorf). Never offer it unless you are fine when he does not take it.

examples.caption: White to move (move 38). The quiet rook move 38.Rd6 seems to leave the f5 pawn to Black's bishop. If 38...Bxf5? then 39.Nd1! attacks the rook on b2 and the bishop on d2 loses its guard (White is winning). Rd6 itself is the strongest move.
examples.source: Fedoseev vs Aravindh, Tata Steel Masters 2026 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-chess-2026-masters/round-13/yuTondoz/9j8aQ18E)

items.title: Tactics beat opening theory
items.text: Most games below master level are decided by tactical blunders, not by opening theory. Spend your time reducing mistakes rather than memorizing tricks.
items.check: Softened: the claim "more than 90%" is the coach's estimate and I could not verify it. It is clearly true that blunders decide most club games.

examples.caption: White to move (move 15). The opening was normal, then Black played 14...Nxc5, grabbing a pawn. 15.dxc5 wins the knight: after 15...Bxd3 16.Qxb7 White is much better. One tactical oversight decided the game, not opening knowledge.
examples.source: Niemann vs Fedoseev, Tata Steel Masters 2026 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-chess-2026-masters/round-1/FRGTkE8Z/nCoDvzh5)

items.title: Look for in-between moves against a pin or threat
items.text: When your opponent sets up an awkward pin or threat (such as a queen move pressing on a diagonal), look for strong in-between moves or counterattacks, such as a mate threat or an attack on a piece, to force them onto the defensive.
items.check: Checked: the in-between move (zwischenzug) is a standard tactic. Make sure the in-between move really forces the issue.

examples.caption: White to move (move 23). Black's rook has just landed on c1, so White's rook and knight are both under pressure. White finds the in-between move Nxf6+ with check, forces gxf6, and only then plays Rxc1. White is winning, while the next best move leaves White clearly worse.

items.title: Keep everything connected and nothing hanging
items.text: Avoid isolated pawns and loose pieces far from the rest of your army. Let pawns and pieces protect each other and stay close, so tactical blunders are reduced to a minimum.
items.check: Checked: "loose pieces drop off" is a classic rule. Weak or flank pawns are best fixed early or connected to the group.

examples.caption: White to move (move 24). After 23...Nc5 Black's bishop on d6 has no defender and the queen is far away on a5. 24.Rxd6 simply takes it (White is clearly better). Loose pieces that do not protect each other get picked off: a punished violation.
examples.source: Praggnanandhaa vs Nepomniachtchi, Candidates 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-candidates-2024-open/round-5/MDiLWQ5M/MI1pR0AA)

items.title: Ask after every move: what does he want?
items.text: After each opponent move ask what the threat or plan is. Run the checks, captures and threats for your opponent as well as for yourself: what could he play next? Parry it in time, for example a pawn advancing in the centre or a threat on the wing, and close their break squares.
items.check: Checked. This keeps you out of hope chess: look first at the intention of the opponent.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 38). Ask what 38.Rd6 wants. The f5 pawn looks free, but after 38...Bxf5? 39.Nd1! hits the rook on b2 and the bishop on d2 loses support (White is winning). 38...Bxc3 removes the knight first and keeps the balance.
examples.source: Fedoseev vs Aravindh, Tata Steel Masters 2026 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-chess-2026-masters/round-13/yuTondoz/9j8aQ18E)

items.title: Tactics flow from a superior position
items.text: Do not hunt desperately for wild combinations or loose tricks. First build a strong, dominant position with space, harmony and active pieces; then the winning tactical blows tend to appear by themselves.
items.check: Softened: a strong guideline, not a law. Tactics still decide when the position is balanced, so keep calculating every move.

examples.caption: White to move (move 29). White has space, a pawn chain on f5 and g5 and active pieces, and Black is passive. The tactical blow 29.Nc6 comes naturally: it hits the rook on d8. It is as strong as 29.g6, and White is clearly better.
examples.source: Caruana vs Dominguez, Sinquefield Cup 2022 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/sinquefield-cup-grand-chess-tour-2022/round-2/rToKKiRI/BkOm9zwH)

items.title: Do not weaken your king shelter lightly
items.text: Castling and keeping the pawns in front of your king in place are about king safety. Do not weaken the king's position for a small material gain, unless enough of your own pieces are close to defend a weakened king.
items.check: Checked.
items.scenario: Try this: before you push a pawn in front of your castled king (f, g or h pawn), ask three questions. Which squares can the opponent's pieces now use? Can my pieces still cover them? Is the material or tempo I gain worth more than that? If you cannot answer yes to the last two, leave the pawns where they are.

items.title: Play actively and take the initiative
items.text: Take the initiative, put your pieces on their best squares, dominate the centre and claim space, without becoming reckless.
items.check: A style, not a rule. Keep calculating: the other principles still apply. Wanting activity is not an excuse to be reckless. Also covers: take the initiative first. As White you have the first move, so use it to create early threats that force a reaction. Softened: Black can take the initiative too, usually a move later. Tie your development to a real or latent threat on the enemy half instead of developing aimlessly.

examples.caption: White to move (move 10). Black has just played ...c5. White answers actively with 10.d5, gaining space in the centre and keeping the initiative instead of a slow move like 10.h3. 10.d5 is the strongest move, and White is slightly better.
examples.source: Gukesh vs Ding Liren, FIDE World Championship Match 2024 Game 7 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-world-championship-2024/game-7/Nax0ffrf/NLdsNZ8e)

items.title: Play forcing, active moves in the opening
items.text: Choose opening moves that develop a minor piece and force an active answer, instead of slow, waiting moves.
items.check: Checked: good, as long as the move is also sound.

examples.caption: White to move (move 4). In this Petroff line 4.Bd3 develops a minor piece and attacks the knight on e4, so Black has to react. It is the strongest move, and White is slightly better. Forcing development beats a slow waiting move.
examples.source: Gukesh vs Abasov, Candidates 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-candidates-2024-open/round-5/MDiLWQ5M/Evh9eivY)

items.title: Do not defend passively out of fear
items.text: Do not play waiting moves out of vague fear, but do respond to concrete threats and prevent the opponent's best plan.
items.check: Checked: but first check the opponent's real threats (see CCTO).

examples.caption: Black to move (move 12). Nothing concrete is threatened, so a just-in-case move like 12...h6 only hands White time and leaves Black slightly worse. Black plays 12...c5, claiming space; the strongest move, with the position equal.
examples.source: Erigaisi vs Keymer, Tata Steel Masters 2025 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-chess-2025-masters/round-10/Cxynl5MH/8xBXUSQh)

items.title: Castle long only when it is safe
items.text: Long castling is the most aggressive form, but only castle long when the position allows it and your king is really safe there.
items.check: Checked: correct. The king is a bit more exposed on the queenside and the pawn cover is thinner.

examples.caption: White to move (move 12). Black has pushed ...b5 and kept his king in the centre, yet White castles long: his pieces cover the queenside and the rook joins the centre. 12.O-O-O is clearly more accurate than 12.f3. Long castling worked because the king was safe.
examples.source: Vidit vs Firouzja, Candidates 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-candidates-2024-open/round-6/kPqEUBZJ/PbcVSZD2)

items.title: Keep fighting for the centre
items.text: Keep the centre in mind and fight for it while it is relevant, by aiming pieces at it or advancing centre pawns. Switch to concrete threats when needed.
items.check: Checked: standard. Also covers: centralization is the key to dominance. Central pieces cover the most squares and push the opponent onto the defensive, so keep pressure on the central squares.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 11). Black keeps fighting for the centre with 11...e5, striking at the d4 pawn instead of waiting. It is the strongest move and the position stays level. The centre is still relevant, so a central pawn break is the right idea.
examples.source: Ding Liren vs Gukesh, FIDE World Championship Match 2024 Game 6 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-world-championship-2024/game-6/I2LcDwAT/aONfLzUf)

items.title: Defend aggressively
items.text: When you have to defend, for example against an attack on your queen, try to answer with an attack of your own on an enemy pawn or piece.
items.check: Checked: a good counterpunch, as long as your counter is real. Also covers: do not panic when the opponent threatens on the wing or in the centre. Look for an active counter-move, an in-between move or a direct threat on their half. Softened: a counterattack only works if it is faster or stronger than the threat. Sometimes the right answer is simply a calm defensive move. Also covers: passive defence is dangerous. It lets the opponent keep attacking undisturbed, so ask: which attacking or countering move can I place on their half?

examples.caption: White to move (move 8). Black's bishop on f5 attacks the queen on c2. Instead of a retreat like 8.Qd1, White answers with 8.Qb3, attacking the b7 pawn at the same time. It is the strongest move and keeps the position equal, while 8.Qd1 leaves White slightly worse.
examples.source: Gukesh vs Ding Liren, FIDE World Championship Match 2024 Game 3 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-world-championship-2024/game-3/RYXkK9po/tEJhDrmj)

items.title: Calculate sacrifices three moves deep
items.text: Calculate a sacrifice as deeply and concretely as you can. If you cannot see clear compensation, do not play it.
items.check: A stricter version from another lesson: calculate the whole line. A sacrifice is right when you end up with more material, or give mate.

examples.caption: White to move (move 32). Qxf7+ Kh8 Bg7+ Nxg7 Qf8+ Rxf8 Rxf8# is a forced mate in four, but it gives up the bishop and then the queen. Every Black reply has to be checked before the first move. Calculate each line to the end; if you cannot see the compensation, do not play it.

items.title: Open the king with a pawn storm
items.text: Advance your pawns (such as the g and h pawns) against the enemy king to open lines and files for your rooks.
items.check: Checked: mainly with opposite-side castling. On the same side it loosens your own king.

examples.caption: White to move (move 13). The kings are on opposite wings: White's is on c1, Black's on g8. White plays g4, the start of a g and h pawn advance meant to open lines against the Black king. g4 is also the strongest move, and Caruana went on to win.
examples.source: Fabiano Caruana vs Matthias Bluebaum, FIDE Candidates 2026, Paphos, round 5, 2026-03-21 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-candidates-2026-open/round-5/liBI9Brw/wuNBfSXX)

items.title: Fix problems with pieces, not pawns
items.text: Prefer piece moves when fixing problems, since pawn moves cannot be undone. A pawn move is fine when it solves a concrete issue (such as h3 or a luft).
items.check: Checked: a good default. A pawn move is sometimes right, for example to make luft.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 23). The bishop on g5 attacks the knight on f6, which stands in front of the rook on d8. The pawn move 23...h6? allows 24.Bxf6 gxf6 and wrecks the king's cover (White is much better). The piece move 23...Ba4 is the strongest move, with White only slightly better.
examples.source: Sarana vs Mendonca, Tata Steel Masters 2025 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/tata-steel-chess-2025-masters/round-13/jRNO3Xth/ot0WnaGS)

items.title: Do not panic and weaken
items.text: When attacked, do not make weakening pawn moves out of panic. Defend accurately and counterattack only if it is really faster.
items.check: Checked: keep calm; only keep pushing when your own attack is real.

examples.caption: White to move (move 25). White's pawn on e5 and queen on g4 hit the knight on h5; Black panicked with the weakening 24...g6?. 25.Ba3! attacks the queen on c5, and the dark squares around the black king are now loose (White is winning).
examples.source: Firouzja vs So, Sinquefield Cup 2022 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/sinquefield-cup-grand-chess-tour-2022/round-8/5iaR9Sei/n3sVkiHw)

items.title: Force reactions with early threats
items.text: Make threats that improve your position while forcing a reaction. Avoid threats that are simply parried, because they only waste time.
items.check: Checked: keeping the initiative works, as long as your threats are real. Also covers: look for moves on the opponent's half that create a direct threat (a check, an annoying pin), so they must react and lose time. Softened: only when the move is sound; a check just to give a check can waste your own tempo.

examples.caption: Applied well. Black (move 11) plays 11...d4, a pawn push that attacks both the knight on c3 and the bishop on e3. White must react at once (the game went 12.Ne4), so the threat is not simply parried and Black gains space. It is the strongest move, and the position is about equal.
examples.source: Sindarov, Javokhir vs Wei, Yi, FIDE World Cup 2025, final game 1 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-world-cup-2025-finals/game-1/ccpVN6xj/dgA9lGPW)

items.title: Avoid hope chess
items.text: Do not play a move hoping your opponent blunders (such as leaving a bishop hanging). Play on objective pressure and concrete calculation.
items.check: Checked: "hope chess" is a known term. A trap is fine when your move is also sound if he does not fall for it (see "Set a trap with a defensive move").

examples.caption: Punished violation. White to move (29) is equal, with quiet moves like a4 or b3. 29.Nc4? puts a knight where the queen can simply take it; it works only if Black misses ...Qxc4 or ...Ng6. Black did not miss it, and Black is winning. Choose moves that survive the best reply.
examples.source: Maghsoodloo, Parham vs Gukesh D, 45th FIDE Olympiad Budapest 2024, Open (https://lichess.org/broadcast/45th-chess-olympiad-budapest-2024-open-i/round-8/cAN0gyPi/4xVVeotf)

items.title: Keep track of the material balance
items.text: Keep the material balance clearly in your head. Every pawn won or lost steers your strategic choices. Being greedy is only fine when it is safe.
items.check: Checked: at club level material matters a lot. Balance it with the poisoned-pawn check: not every free pawn is free.

examples.caption: Punished greed. Black (move 11) can win a pawn with 11...Qxb2. But the queen leaves the centre while the king is still on e8 and the rook and bishop are undeveloped. White gets Na4 and Rab1 with tempo, and White goes from clearly better to winning. A pawn is only worth taking when it is safe; 11...Be7 was better.
examples.source: Prohaszka, Peter vs Aoshima, Mirai, 45th FIDE Olympiad Budapest 2024, Open (https://lichess.org/broadcast/45th-chess-olympiad-budapest-2024-open-i/round-4/6wJduA1I/VQWrIkki)

items.title: Use advanced pawns as wedges
items.text: Advanced pawns can cramp the opponent when they are well supported and your king is not at risk. Calculate before you push.
items.check: Softened: an advanced pawn needs support, or it becomes a target. Calculate the risks to your own king before you push.

examples.caption: White to move (move 31). Black's pieces are short of room. Karpov pushes f5, a pawn backed by e4, which shuts the kingside and leaves Black's pieces with few squares. White's king is safe. f5 is the strongest move and leaves White much better, against only a clear edge for quieter tries.
examples.source: Karpov vs Unzicker, Nice Olympiad 1974 (https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1067846)

items.title: Activity can be worth more than material
items.text: Activity can compensate for material when it creates concrete threats. Check it with calculation, and check that the opponent cannot safely return the material.
