items.check: Softened: a guideline for calculated sacrifices. Unsound sacrifices lose; check that the pressure is lasting and that the opponent has no safe way to return the material.

examples.caption: White to move (move 14). Karpov plays h5, offering the h-pawn. After ...Nxh5 g4 the knight is chased back and White's pieces and pawns become very active. Even a pawn down, White is still clearly better, and h5 is nearly as accurate as g4.
examples.source: Karpov vs Korchnoi, Candidates Final, Moscow 1974 (https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1067858)

items.title: Judge activity by squares controlled and mobility
items.text: Activity means the number of squares you control and the dynamic value of your pieces. If you win a passive rook or piece in a corner but lose your active bishops and knights for it, you give away valuable dominance. Keep active pieces on the board and push the opponent into a passive role.
items.check: Softened: activity is not a replacement for material. Count both, and check how long the activity lasts. Also covers: activity is not only the number of squares a piece controls, but which squares it reaches on the opponent's half. Improve it by manoeuvring pieces to better squares, moving your own blocking pawns, or opening the structure with a pawn break.

examples.caption: Black to move (13). Counting material says 13...Rxc3 is a mistake: a rook for a knight. Counting activity says otherwise. After bxc3 White's rooks are shut in behind their own pawns and a broken queenside, while Black keeps both knights and both bishops on active squares. Rxc3 is the strongest move, and Black is clearly better.
examples.source: Esipenko, Andrey vs Caruana, Fabiano, FIDE Candidates 2026, round 14 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-candidates-2026-open/round-14/oBkeHnpi/gi2VX6NQ)

items.title: Opposite-side castling is a race
items.text: When the kings castle on opposite sides, speed and mating attacks matter most. The player who starts a pawn storm first, with enough pieces behind it, usually gets the better of it.
items.check: Softened: the first version said the first storm almost always wins. Tempo is key, but development and counterplay in the centre still matter.

examples.caption: White to move (move 17). The kings are on opposite wings, so speed counts. Black's queenside pawns are already moving (...b4), and Fischer starts his own storm with h4. White is clearly better, and h4 is close to the most accurate move, a3.
examples.source: Fischer vs Larsen, Portoroz Interzonal 1958 (https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1008373)

items.title: Support the pawn storm
items.text: A pawn storm works best when the leading pawn is supported by pieces or pawns, so that lines really open.
items.check: Checked: a pawn storm needs a supported spearhead, so the leading pawn is backed by a second pawn or a piece.

examples.caption: White to move (move 21). Kings are on opposite wings. White's g-pawn has the f3 pawn, the queen and both rooks behind it. 21.g5 kicks the knight and is clearly the strongest move, leaving White much better; a quiet move like Qd3 leaves the position about equal.
examples.source: Fischer vs Larsen, Portoroz Interzonal 1958 (https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1008373)

items.title: Answer a wing attack in the centre
items.text: If a faster pawn storm hits one wing, look for counterplay by opening the centre. This often changes the course of the game and defuses the wing attack.
items.check: Checked: a classical principle. Also covers: counter a premature flank attack by striking at once in the centre (for example with d4). Central pieces have the most power and force the opponent to defend. Softened: only when your pieces are developed enough to support the break.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 12). White is storming the kingside with g4-g5 while the kings are on opposite sides. Fischer answers in the centre with ...d4, hitting the knight on c3 and bishop on e3. It is the strongest move, and Black is clearly better.
examples.source: Grossguth vs Fischer, US Junior Championship 1956 (https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1008359)

items.title: Open lines by trading pawns
items.text: A pawn storm aims to open lines for your rooks and queen by trading pawns. Removing the pawns around the enemy king exposes the defence and makes quick mating patterns possible.
items.check: Checked: correct. Also covers: an attack stalls in a closed position. To make it succeed, open the position, preferably with a controlled pawn break, otherwise with a strong sacrifice, once your pieces are ready to enter.

examples.caption: White to move (move 19). Fischer plays hxg6. After ...hxg6 the h-file is open and his rooks aim straight at Black's king. 19.hxg6 leaves White clearly better and is nearly as accurate as g4. Trading pawns near the king opens lines for the heavy pieces.
examples.source: Fischer vs Larsen, Portoroz Interzonal 1958 (https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1008373)

items.title: Prepare the pawn storm
items.text: Do not push a pawn when the opponent can place a blocking knight in front of it and slow you down. Check that knight's landing square before you move the pawn mass forward.
items.check: Checked: correct.

examples.caption: Punished violation. White (move 30) pushes 30.e5?, but Black's knight on c7 can hop to e6, right in front of the pawn. The blockade stops the pawn mass and e5 becomes something to defend. Quiet moves like Rxd4 or Ne2 leave White slightly worse; after e5 Ne6 White is much worse. Check the knight's landing square first.
examples.source: Bartel, Mateusz vs Sosa, Tomas, 45th FIDE Olympiad Budapest 2024, Open (https://lichess.org/broadcast/45th-chess-olympiad-budapest-2024-open-i/round-3/5tLXKIAf/sBxTa1gc)

items.title: Exchange sacrifice on the wing
items.text: An exchange sacrifice (rook for a minor piece) can break open the king position when it gives lasting attacking chances.
items.check: Softened: only when you can calculate it. The original called it forcing, which is not true in general. This also goes against 'simple, controlled play', so use it only with a clear calculation.

examples.caption: White to move (move 22). Fischer gives a rook for a knight with Rxh5. After ...gxh5 the g-pawn is free to run with g6, and Black's king is stripped of cover. Rxh5 leaves White clearly better, while the quiet Bxg7 is already slightly worse for White.
examples.source: Fischer vs Larsen, Portoroz Interzonal 1958 (https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1008373)

items.title: Tighten the net with flank pawns (f3, g4, h4)
items.text: Flank pawn advances can trap a piece or gain space when your own king is safe. Check concrete lines first.
items.check: Checked: a real tactic (trapping a piece on the edge). Check your own king safety first: these pawn moves also open lines near your own king.

examples.caption: White to move (move 15). With his king safe on c1, Karpov already has f3 and now plays g4, kicking the knight on h5 and gaining space on the kingside. It is the strongest move and leaves White clearly better; the quiet Nce2 gives only a slight edge.
examples.source: Karpov vs Korchnoi, Candidates Final, Moscow 1974 (https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1067858)

items.title: Coordinate knights and rooks for mate
items.text: Bring knights and rooks along open files to advanced squares (such as f4) to create deadly mating patterns on the back rank or around the enemy king.
items.check: Checked: a core attacking idea. The "f4" square comes from one example, so it is generalized here.

examples.caption: White to move (move 23). The queen is on h6 and the rook on the h-file. Karpov brings the second knight to f4 with Nef4, so both knights, queen and rook point at Black's king. It is by far the strongest move and White is winning, while the alternatives Nxf6+ and Kb1 leave White slightly worse.
examples.source: Karpov vs Korchnoi, Candidates Final, Moscow 1974 (https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1067858)

items.title: Be patient in an attack
items.text: Sometimes you should prepare a position calmly (for example with g6 or a quiet regrouping) to build maximum pressure, rather than playing hasty forcing tactics the opponent can parry.
items.check: Checked: good advice. Softened: if a forcing line is calculated and works, play it. Also covers: coordinate as a connected team before the final attack. A loose attack with too few active pieces fails against good defence. First harmony and centre control, then forcing combinations and sacrifices.

examples.caption: White to move (22). Hasty tries such as Qh5 or Qg3 trade queens or get parried, and they leave White clearly worse. White instead plays the calm 22.g6, undermining the king's cover and keeping every piece for the next phase (Bf3, Rae1 follow). It is the only move that keeps White much better.
examples.source: Mastrovasilis, Dimitrios vs Banh Gia Huy, 46th FIDE Olympiad Samarkand 2026, Open (https://lichess.org/broadcast/46th-fide-chess-olympiad-samarkand-2026-open-matches-13-37/round-3/3xi4XaHj/3d0U2Wmq)

items.title: Watch for long-range snipers
items.text: Always watch for distant pieces (a bishop or rook on a long diagonal or file) that strike from afar, to avoid tactical blunders and back-rank problems.
items.check: Checked: long-range pieces are easy to overlook. Look along every long diagonal and open file.

examples.caption: Punished violation. White (move 38) grabs the pawn with 38.Qxe4?? and forgets the rook on d6, far away on the open d-file, aimed at d1 where the king and rook are stuck on the back rank. Black plays ...Rd1+, the knight must take, and the queen on e4 falls. Safe was 38.Rg3, which keeps the position equal.
examples.source: Caruana, Fabiano vs Nakamura, Hikaru, Norway Chess 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2024-open/round-1/I9TLGEOt/hkSR1sG5)

items.title: Clear the way for a kingside attack (f4 or d4)
items.text: Prepare the f4 break (or a central d4 break) in closed positions to activate your pieces.
items.check: Checked: a typical plan in closed centres. Prepare it first, and check the pawn weaknesses it creates.

examples.caption: White to move (move 30). The centre is closed, and Karpov has put his knights on e2 and h2 to prepare the f4 break. 30.f4 opens the f-file and activates his pieces; it is the strongest move, leaving White clearly better, against a slightly smaller edge for Bc2.
examples.source: Karpov vs Unzicker, Nice Olympiad 1974 (https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1067846)

items.title: Use the bishop pair against weak dark squares
items.text: If you keep the bishop pair, or trade off the enemy defenders, you can invade the weakened squares (such as the dark squares around the enemy king) step by step.
items.check: Checked: a standard strategic theme.

examples.caption: Applied well. White (move 34) still has both bishops while Black has no bishop at all, so the dark squares around the Black king (g5, h6, f6) have no defender. 34.Qh6+ steps in, and after ...Kh8 the dark-squared bishop follows with Bg5 (White is winning). White did not rush; the dark squares were taken one by one.
examples.source: Petkov, Momchil vs Momin, Fayzan, 45th FIDE Olympiad Budapest 2024, Open (https://lichess.org/broadcast/45th-chess-olympiad-budapest-2024-open-i/round-1/XJ8g9CkA/gGtV0S7D)

items.title: Use opposite-coloured bishops as an attacking weapon
items.text: In a middlegame with opposite-coloured bishops, your bishop works like an extra attacker that your opponent cannot challenge. Use it to find and hit weaknesses around the enemy king.
items.check: Checked: true in the middlegame. In the endgame the same bishops tend to draw (see the warning above).

examples.caption: Applied well. White's bishop on h6 is dark-squared; Black's bishop on d7 is light-squared, so it can never contest the dark squares around the king, and White's bishop acts like an extra attacker. White (move 30) plays 30.Re7+ Kg8 31.Qc4+ Kh8 32.Bg7#. It is mate in four, the strongest move.
examples.source: Alekhine, Alexander vs Baljet, Lindenaar, simultaneous display, Bandung, 1933 (pgnmentor.com/players/Alekhine.zip)

items.title: Bring your rooks into the game
items.text: In the heat of an attack players often forget their rooks on a1 or h1. Make sure every piece joins the attack, and before a serious attack check that your rooks and heavy pieces have left their starting squares.
items.check: Checked: a very common mistake at club level. Also covers: before a decisive attack every piece, including bishops and rooks on the back rank, must take part. Check for passive pieces in your own camp and bring them to open files or central squares.

examples.caption: After 12.O-O-O, both white rooks take part in the attack at once (Rd1 pins the d7 knight, Rh1 supports). Black's rooks are still sleeping. White is winning. Source: Opera Game (Morphy vs Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard, Paris 1858).

items.title: Do not respect an unsupported attack
items.text: If the opponent sets up a threat or pin early with a single piece (such as an isolated bishop) while the rest of the army stays passive, do not panic or turn passive. An attack is only dangerous when they outnumber you there. Count the real attackers and defenders on that part of the board first, then respond calmly.
items.check: Checked. Softened: a single piece can still win material with a tactic, so check the concrete threat first.

examples.caption: Applied well. Black's bishop on b4 pins the knight on c3, but it is the only Black piece involved; the rest of the army is still at home. White (move 6) counts attackers, stays calm and simply develops with 6.Nf3. The position stays about equal. A single pinning piece is not an attack.
examples.source: Gukesh D vs Carlsen, Magnus, Norway Chess 2026, Open (https://lichess.org/broadcast/norway-chess-2026-open/round-4/qm5sMu4C/umjqU9Ty)

items.title: Trade off the key attackers
items.text: When the opponent builds pressure with only a few active pieces, the quickest road to safety is to trade exactly those pieces. Once the attackers are gone, the attack collapses and you can take over the initiative.
items.check: Checked. Make sure the trade does not open a file or diagonal for their remaining pieces.

examples.caption: Applied well. White's pressure rests on very few pieces: the bishop on d5, backed by the pawn on c6, and the queen. Black (move 28) simply trades the key attacker with 28...Bxd5. After cxd5 the pressure is gone and Black's rook and queen take over the open files; the position is equal, and the trade is the best move.
examples.source: Avila Pavas, Santiago vs Zilka, Stepan, 45th FIDE Olympiad Budapest 2024, Open (https://lichess.org/broadcast/45th-chess-olympiad-budapest-2024-open-i/round-7/CphdUotb/GdMw0NOa)

items.title: Plant a piece deep in the enemy camp
items.text: A well-supported piece on an outpost deep in the enemy camp can paralyse the opponent. Check first that it cannot be removed.
items.check: Softened: the planted piece must be hard to dislodge or must win something concrete. Otherwise it is simply lost material.

examples.caption: White to move (move 24). Karpov puts his bishop on a7, deep in Black's camp. Black's rook cannot take it, because the rook on a2 recaptures, and the bishop cramps Black's pieces on the queenside. It is the strongest move, and White is clearly better.
examples.source: Karpov vs Unzicker, Nice Olympiad 1974 (https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1067846)

items.title: In an attack, time can be worth more than material
items.text: The aim of a sacrifice is often not direct mate but time: slowing the opponent's development and locking their position in passivity. Accept a material sacrifice when it forces the opponent to spend tempi on defence instead of development.
items.check: Checked. Calculate concretely: time is only worth it if you can keep the initiative until the pressure pays off.

examples.caption: White to move (move 10). Black has a knight and rook still at home and a king in the centre. Morphy plays Nxb5, giving a knight for a pawn to keep Black busy defending instead of developing. It is the strongest move: White is winning, against only a clear edge for the safe Bxf6.
examples.source: Morphy vs Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard, Paris 1858 (move list: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opera_Game)

items.title: Count the pieces in the fight, not on the board
items.text: Do not worry about lost pawns or pieces if the pieces that remain are passive spectators. If you concentrate all your active forces on one wing, you win the numbers there. Judge a position by how many active pieces take part, not only by the material balance.
items.check: Checked. Softened: material still counts in the long run, especially if the opponent can bring their pieces back in time.

examples.caption: White (move 24) is a full exchange down: Black has two rooks against one. But count the pieces that can play. Black's rooks on c8 and e8 and the bishop on f8 are boxed in, while White's queen, rook, knight and bishop all aim at the king. 24.Nf5 keeps the pressure; White is still much better.
examples.source: Nakamura, Hikaru vs Firouzja, Alireza, FIDE Candidates 2022, round 10 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-candidates-tournament-2022/round-10/FWJYzJJJ/p6WTG2T6)

items.title: Launch a massive attack only when you outnumber the defenders
items.text: Start a large attack not because you feel like it, but when you can show that you have more attackers than they have defenders near the king. Build up methodically, then open the position.
items.check: Checked. The counterpart of: do not respect an unsupported attack.

examples.caption: Applied well. White (move 31) has rook, queen, bishop and knight all aimed at the Black king on e7. Black's only nearby defender is the bishop on e8, with the queen and rook far away on the a-file. Count: four attackers against about one. Only now does White open the position with 31.Rxe6+! (White is winning).
examples.source: Kramnik, Vladimir vs Carlsen, Magnus, Sparkassen GM Dortmund, 2009 (pgnmentor.com/players/Carlsen.zip)

items.title: Punish a king stuck in the centre
items.text: If the opponent fails to castle in time and leaves the king in the middle, often behind a weakened pawn shield such as e6 and f7, act at once: open the centre and create strong threats, with a sacrifice if needed.
items.check: Softened: only when you are better developed. If your own pieces are not out yet, opening the centre can backfire.

examples.caption: White to move after 9...b5. White has developed fast, Black's king is still in the middle and Black's queenside pieces are not out. 10.Nxb5! opens the position at once (White is winning). Source: Opera Game (Morphy vs Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard, Paris 1858).

items.title: Eliminate the key defenders of the king
items.text: An attack often fails because specific key pieces (such as a bishop or a defending knight) hold the enemy king together. To make the attack succeed, deliberately remove or deflect those key defenders.
items.check: Checked. See also: remove the defending bishop.

examples.caption: White to move after 12...Rd8. The knight on d7 is the key defender: it blocks the d-file and guards the king. 13.Rxd7! Rxd7 14.Rd1 and the pin wins (White is winning). Source: Opera Game (Morphy vs Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard, Paris 1858).

items.title: Use a pawn as an umbrella when under pressure
items.text: Under pressure, a well-defended pawn can block enemy lines or cramp attackers. Check that it does not become a target.
items.check: Softened: the term is used in different ways; this describes the effect. Check that the pawn itself can be defended, or it just becomes a target.

examples.caption: Applied well. Black (move 23) is under pressure: the bishop on h4 pins the knight on e7 to the queen. 23...f6 puts a pawn on that line as an umbrella. It is guarded by the knight on h5, and it is safe as a target: after fxe5, ...dxe5. It is the strongest move, and the position is about equal.
examples.source: Rapport, Richard vs Ding, Liren, FIDE Candidates 2022, round 10 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-candidates-tournament-2022/round-10/FWJYzJJJ/MQbOh83j)

items.title: Trade pieces when ahead
items.text: With a material lead, trading pieces is the fastest way to win. Fewer pieces make it easier to cash in. Trade pieces, not pawns.
items.check: Checked: correct. Be careful with fortress positions. Other lessons say the same: fewer pieces make your extra material weigh more. Another lesson adds: do it once your opponent's attack is neutralized. Softened: it is not completely risk-free. One pawn up is enough to simplify, but see the opposite-coloured bishops warning. When you are behind, avoid needless trades. Another lesson: if you won a piece or the exchange, trade methodically (the minor pieces first) to simplify and steer the endgame to a win.

examples.caption: White to move (move 37). Fischer is a piece up. He trades queens with Qxd8, removing Black's most dangerous piece and keeping the extra material. It is the strongest move; ...Rxd8 Rxc5 follows and White's lead stays big.
examples.source: Fischer vs Feuerstein, US Championship 1957/58 (https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1008369)

items.title: Create a passed pawn
items.text: Use a pawn majority on one wing to create a passed pawn. A passed pawn ties down the opponent and often decides the endgame.
items.check: Once you have broken up your opponent's structure, creating a passed pawn and pushing it (best close to promotion) is the fastest way to put them on the defensive. Softened: another lesson says an equal endgame is won almost only by a passed pawn. It is the most common way, but king activity and winning pawns win games too. Softened: "endgames are won by passed pawns" is a strong guideline, not a law. With fewer pieces a mating attack becomes unlikely, so the creation and support of a passed pawn, together with an active king, becomes the main winning plan.

examples.caption: White to move (move 44). White has three pawns (e, f, h) against two (f, h) on the kingside. exf6 removes Black's f-pawn and leaves White with a passed pawn on f6 that ties down the bishop and king. exf6 leaves White winning, while the other moves are roughly equal.
examples.source: Giri vs Niemann, FIDE Grand Swiss, Samarkand 2025, round 11 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-grand-swiss-2025-open/round-11/pAVa5HIv/pxQ6cwOU)

items.title: Rook versus minor piece: win it with technique
items.text: Being up the exchange is a real edge, worth about 1.5 to 2 pawns. Build calmly, activate your king and use the rook to pick up pawns.
items.check: Corrected: it is not automatically won. In the middlegame it usually wins with a pawn or more; in endgames with blocked pawns or no pawns the minor piece can draw.

examples.caption: White to move (move 61). White is up the exchange, a rook against a knight, with equal pawns. There is no rush: Kc4 brings the king forward first, and the rook will then pick up weak pawns such as those on b6 and c6. Kc4 is the strongest move, and White is winning.
examples.source: Amin vs Suyarov, FIDE Grand Swiss, Samarkand 2025, round 6 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-grand-swiss-2025-open/round-6/iAnC0jAl/svAhb55h)

items.title: Activate your king in the endgame
items.text: In the endgame the king is a strong piece, not a target. Bring it to the centre to support your pawns and block the opponent.
items.check: Checked: true once queens are off and there is no mating danger. Another lesson adds: a central king supports your passed pawns and cuts off the enemy king. Another lesson says the same: once the queens are gone, march the king to the centre. Active defensive squares count too (such as e2) as soon as the middlegame is over.

examples.caption: White to move (move 60). Only bishops and pawns are left, so the king is safe and strong. Kf4 starts the march to e5, where it attacks the d5 pawn and supports White's own pawns. In the game the king reached e5 and Black lost the d5 pawn. Kf4 is practically the strongest move, and White is winning.
examples.source: Oparin vs Daneshvar, FIDE Grand Swiss, Samarkand 2025, round 2 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-grand-swiss-2025-open/round-2/UnZivDF9/xQP5Fx6R)

items.title: Push your passed pawn
items.text: Push the passed pawn when it is supported and cannot be stopped easily. Passed pawns must be pushed, but with piece support.
items.check: Checked: a standard rule. Do not run it unsupported and watch for the enemy king. Priority number one in an endgame when it can run unhindered: push it, but in a controlled way.

examples.caption: White to move (move 42). White's d-pawn is passed and the rook on a6 backs it up along the sixth rank. d6 pushes it to a square the rook protects and next to the seventh rank, so Black's rook and king are tied to stopping it. d6 is the strongest move, and White is winning.
examples.source: Hakobyan vs Shankland, FIDE Grand Swiss, Samarkand 2025, round 8 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-grand-swiss-2025-open/round-8/KaLeVROn/Den3ogcF)

items.title: Put your pawns on the opposite colour of the enemy bishop
items.text: Against a bishop, pawns on the opposite colour are safe from it. Keep your own pawns on the colour opposite your own bishop.
items.check: Corrected: the title said 'same colour', but the rule is the opposite colour of his bishop. It makes the bishop much weaker, not completely useless.

examples.caption: Applied well, from White's side (move 41). White's bishop is light-squared and all White pawns (c3, d4, h2) stand on dark squares, so the knight cannot attack them. Black's pawns on b7, d5 and g4 all sit on light squares, in the bishop's line of fire. 41.Kxg4 wins one at once (White is winning).
examples.source: Mattaaq, Egon vs Johnson, Nicholas, 46th FIDE Olympiad Samarkand 2026, Open (https://lichess.org/broadcast/46th-fide-chess-olympiad-samarkand-2026-open-matches-88/round-5/JqG93N2H/8gwyOzOl)

items.title: Mate with king and queen
items.text: Shrink the box around the enemy king with your queen a knight's move away, bring your own king up, and finish with the 'kiss of death' or a corner mate. Check for stalemate on every move.
items.check: Checked: always wins if you avoid stalemate. Wording: 'mirroring' became 'a knight's move away'.

examples.caption: White to move (move 95). The queen on b3 already walls off the b-file, so the Black king is boxed on the a-file. White brings the king up with 95.Kc6 and mate follows next move (96.Qb6# after ...Ka6). Pick moves that shrink the box and always check Black still has a legal move, so you avoid stalemate.
examples.source: Fofana, Aguibou vs Chottu, Melanie, 46th FIDE Olympiad Samarkand 2026, Open (https://lichess.org/broadcast/46th-fide-chess-olympiad-samarkand-2026-open-matches-88/round-4/qBGGiwfo/J8EPb9DK)

items.title: Trade queens when you are a pawn up
items.text: With a pawn extra, trading queens is often a good way to simplify and make a setback unlikely.
items.check: Softened: often right, not always. A queenless endgame can still be drawn, and check the trade does not give the opponent compensation.

examples.caption: White to move (move 34). White is a clean pawn up with queen and knight each. Qxe6 fxe6 trades queens, leaves Black with a weak e6 pawn and an exposed b4 pawn, and removes any counterplay against the white king. It is the strongest move, and White is winning.
examples.source: Daneshvar vs Muradli, FIDE Grand Swiss, Samarkand 2025, round 7 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-grand-swiss-2025-open/round-7/xtmbmvSP/hcCGVN0R)

examples.caption: Black to move (move 47). Black has four pawns against three. Qxf3+ Kxf3 trades queens and leaves a rook ending where the extra pawn and the more active rook count, and the white king has no attack left. It is the strongest move, and Black is winning.
examples.source: Atalik vs Mamedyarov, 41st European Chess Club Cup, 2026, round 2 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/41st-european-chess-club-cup-2026-open/round-2/ETE9LeyG/hzZBsppG)

items.title: Pieces first, then pawns
items.text: Usually activate your king and pieces first. When a pawn race decides, count it concretely.
items.check: Softened: usually. In pawn races, speed can matter more.

examples.caption: White to move (move 48). White has a far-advanced passed pawn on d6, but pushing it at once with d7 is only about equal, as the rook can deal with it. Kd5 first brings the king up to support the pawn, and White is winning. In the game White played Kd5, Kc6 and only then d7.
examples.source: Sindarov vs Hovhannisyan, FIDE Grand Swiss, Samarkand 2025, round 7 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-grand-swiss-2025-open/round-7/xtmbmvSP/1u3VXRcU)

items.title: Fewer pawn islands
items.text: Fewer pawn islands are easier to defend. Keep your pawns connected.
items.check: Corrected: the idea is right. The exact rule depends on the position: recapture with the pawn or the piece that keeps your pawns together, not always with a piece.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 63). Both sides have five pawns, but Black's form one connected chain from b7 to f4, while White's are split into three islands, with a2 and g5 left alone. fxe3+ opens the way for the e-pawn and Black's pawns protect each other. It is the strongest move, and Black is winning.
examples.source: Gelfand vs Praggnanandhaa, FIDE Grand Swiss, Samarkand 2025, round 3 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-grand-swiss-2025-open/round-3/gLwN3kib/lVQ1lhIB)

items.title: Beware opposite-coloured bishops
items.text: Be careful trading into an endgame with opposite-coloured bishops when you are only one pawn up. The defender can often draw easily.
items.check: Checked: correct. With queens and rooks on the board, opposite bishops can help the attacker instead.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 35). White has five pawns against four, but the bishops live on opposite colours, so White cannot attack Black's pawns with the bishop and Black can build a fortress. The position is about equal, and the game ended in a draw.
examples.source: Gukesh D vs Ding Liren, FIDE World Championship Match game 5, Singapore 2024 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-world-championship-2024/game-5/57VhOk8z/g5jsHWxW)

items.title: Castling is not automatic without queens
items.text: When queens are off, your king is in less danger. Do not castle out of habit: use the king in the centre to fight and support pawns.
items.check: Checked: castling is just no longer a priority. Also: a short-castled king in the corner can get boxed in and loses tempi getting to the centre. Softened from "almost never": it is just rarely worth the time. Another lesson repeats this: do not castle out of habit when queens left the board early. A king in the corner takes no part in the game. Do not be lured by strong players who still castle short long after the queens are off. Their king ends up in a useless corner instead of the active centre.

examples.caption: White to move (move 17). Queens are already off the board, so the king is not in danger. Instead of castling by habit, White plays Kf2, keeping the king near the centre where it can support its pawns and join the fight. Kf2 is more accurate than castling kingside, though both leave White only slightly better.
examples.source: Giri vs Niemann, FIDE Grand Swiss, Samarkand 2025, round 11 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-grand-swiss-2025-open/round-11/pAVa5HIv/pxQ6cwOU)

items.title: Doubled isolated pawns are a target
items.text: Aim for positions where the opponent gets doubled, isolated pawns. They are hard to defend and easy to attack in the endgame.
items.check: Checked and aligned with the doubled-pawn principle above: it is the isolation and blocking that make them weak. You can also trade at the right moment to give your opponent doubled pawns, which are permanent targets. The other side of it: do not be scared of doubled pawns of your own. In open positions they can strengthen your control of the centre and compensate for the loss of a bishop.

examples.caption: White to move (move 46). Black has doubled, isolated pawns on h5 and h4. gxh4 wins one at once, and the other on h5 has no neighbour pawn to protect it. White's bishop and king then outplay the knight. gxh4 is the strongest move, and White is winning.
examples.source: Giri vs Van Foreest, FIDE Grand Swiss, Samarkand 2025, round 9 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-grand-swiss-2025-open/round-9/FpwTKfvI/Vc7QJqJD)

items.title: Shelter your king from checks
items.text: In rook endings, put your king behind your own pawns so the enemy rook cannot keep giving checks.
items.check: Checked: a known technique. Balance it with an active king when there are no annoying checks. In won rook endings you can hide king and rook behind or between your own pawns, so that the enemy rook cannot give permanent checks.

examples.caption: White to move (move 41). The g6 and h7 pawns can cover White's king. Kg5 heads for that shelter, so Black's rook runs out of useful checks, while Rb8+ and h8 promotion are threatened. Kg5 is by far the strongest move, and White is winning. In the game: 41...Re2 42.Rb8+ Kg7 43.h8=B mate.
examples.source: Liang vs Theodorou, FIDE Grand Swiss, Samarkand 2025, round 10 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-grand-swiss-2025-open/round-10/ytyOPXN7/9CkEsOyr)

items.title: Watch out for stalemate
items.text: When your pawn is about to promote and the enemy king is boxed in, make sure your opponent still has a legal move.
items.check: Checked: stalemate turns wins into draws. In won endgames stay alert until the last move so you do not take away all legal moves before you give mate.

examples.caption: White to move (move 99). White has a rook against a pawn and Black's king on h2 is boxed in. The careless Kf1 would leave Black with no legal move: stalemate and a draw. Rg3 keeps one legal move for Black (Kh1), and Rxh3 is mate next. So Rg3 gives mate in two. White played it.
examples.source: Martirosyan vs Wagner, FIDE Grand Swiss, Samarkand 2025, round 5 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-grand-swiss-2025-open/round-5/ADzdjVmn/605NKsEm)

items.title: Stay careful until the last move
items.text: Even in a won endgame one slip can throw away the win or allow a draw. Keep calculating and look for the cleanest forced finish.
items.check: Calculate to the very last move: a wrong king square against a mate threat can turn a won position into a loss.

examples.caption: Black to move (move 58). Black is clearly better with an h3 pawn, a knight and a rook against a rook; Rg3 keeps Black much better. Black played Kg5 instead, and the position is equal afterwards. The game ended in a draw. One careless move can throw away a won position.
examples.source: Eren vs Smeets, 41st European Chess Club Cup, 2026, round 3 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/41st-european-chess-club-cup-2026-open/round-3/4mEzILI0/NurUp898)

items.title: The scissor technique with a bishop
items.text: In the endgame one bishop can sometimes control two enemy passed pawns at once by standing on the right diagonal, as long as you calculate precisely.
items.check: Draft: I could not confirm the name. The idea only works in specific positions. It needs a concrete example before it gets its own page.

items.title: March a pawn majority
items.text: With a pawn majority on the queenside (4 against 2, for example), use it to advance your pawns step by step into a passed pawn and force your opponent into passive defence.
items.check: Checked: a standard endgame plan. Keep the pawns supported and watch the enemy king.

examples.caption: White to move (move 53). On the kingside White has three pawns (e4, f4, g2) against two (e5, h5), and Black's king is far away on the queenside. f5 starts the march: the pawns advance together toward a passed pawn, supported by the knight and king. f5 is the strongest move, and White is winning.
examples.source: Haring vs Ostergaard, 41st European Chess Club Cup, 2026, round 3 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/41st-european-chess-club-cup-2026-open/round-3/4mEzILI0/oqJs9b9Z)

items.title: Keep the opponent's pieces passive
items.text: When the opponent's rook is tied to passive defence, trade off their active pieces and centralise your own. Steer towards an endgame where the passive piece stays a problem for them.
items.check: Checked: sound, as long as the endgame you reach is actually better for you.

examples.caption: White to move (move 34). Black's rook sits on a8 doing one job: guarding the a6 pawn. Rd5 centralises White's rook, eyes a5 and keeps the black rook on passive duty. In the game Black tried 34...Rc8 and White went 35.Ra5 to hit a6. Rd5 is the strongest move, and White is winning.
examples.source: Karthikeyan vs Pasti, 41st European Chess Club Cup, 2026, round 5 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/41st-european-chess-club-cup-2026-open/round-5/zd7N7QUW/3ClQtqyW)

items.title: Trade down when the structure is equal
items.text: Trade down when the endgame favours you (better king, structure or activity), or when a draw is acceptable.
items.check: Checked: good for a safe game. If you need to win, keep the tension instead.

examples.caption: White to move (move 67). Material is equal, two pawns each, but White's king is far more active on e5. Bxc6 Kxc6 trades bishops into a king-and-pawn ending where that king dominates. Bxc6 leaves White winning, while the other bishop moves are only about equal.
examples.source: Oparin vs Daneshvar, FIDE Grand Swiss, Samarkand 2025, round 2 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-grand-swiss-2025-open/round-2/UnZivDF9/xQP5Fx6R)

items.title: Convert with an outside passed pawn
items.text: With extra pawns in a late middlegame, trade in a controlled way, create a distant (outside) passed pawn and force your opponent onto the defensive.
items.check: Checked: an outside passed pawn pulls the enemy king away and is a classic winning method.

examples.caption: White to move (move 47). White's a-pawn is a distant passed pawn, far from Black's king and kingside pawns. a5 pushes it and forces the knight and king to react on the wing. a5 is the strongest move and leaves White much better, while quieter moves leave only a slight edge.
examples.source: Hovhannisyan vs Fedoseev, FIDE Grand Swiss, Samarkand 2025, round 3 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-grand-swiss-2025-open/round-3/gLwN3kib/9XM3RK7Z)

items.title: Attack the opponent's pawns in the endgame
items.text: In the endgame there is usually too little attacking material left to mate. Pawns cannot run away, so make the weak or isolated pawns of the opponent the target of your rooks and king.
items.check: Checked. Softened: "too little to mate" holds mostly in minor-piece and rook endings; with queens on, king safety still matters. Also covers: the goal changes. In the middlegame you hunt the king; in the endgame there is too little attacking material, so aim all your firepower at the weak pawns.

examples.caption: White to move (move 35). Black's a6 pawn is isolated and nothing guards it. Ra5 attacks it at once and forces the black rook to passive defence, so White's king and pawns can improve. No mating attack is needed: the pawn is the target. Ra5 is the strongest move, and White is winning.
examples.source: Karthikeyan vs Pasti, 41st European Chess Club Cup, 2026, round 5 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/41st-european-chess-club-cup-2026-open/round-5/zd7N7QUW/3ClQtqyW)

items.title: Prefer the bishop with pawns on both wings
items.text: In endgames with pawns on both sides of the board a bishop is usually better than a knight, because it works on both wings at once and across the whole board, while a knight can operate on only one side at a time.
items.check: Corrected: "superior" was too strong. It is a small, general edge. In closed positions with pawns locked on the bishop's colour, a knight can be just as good or better.

examples.caption: White to move (move 36). Pawns are equal and sit on both wings, and Black's knight is stuck on the rim at a3. Bxe5 wins the centre pawn, and from e5 the bishop also eyes g7 on the other side of the board. A knight cannot guard both wings. Bxe5 is the strongest move, and White is winning.
examples.source: Giri vs Van Foreest, FIDE Grand Swiss, Samarkand 2025, round 9 (https://lichess.org/broadcast/fide-grand-swiss-2025-open/round-9/FpwTKfvI/Vc7QJqJD)

items.title: Set a psychological opening bait
items.text: In specific openings you can leave a seemingly unprotected piece or pawn as bait (for example your queen on c2 or b3 against an early ...Qb6) and tempt your opponent into a fatal mistake by looking patient.
items.check: Checked: baits are a known club tactic. The exact position in the source is unclear, so no example yet. Works mainly against weaker players or in blitz; against strong players rely on sound moves.
items.scenario: Try this: choose a line where a natural-looking mistake loses quickly (an opening trap), and play it for a month in rapid games. Keep track of how often the opponent falls for it and what they do when they do not. Know your own follow-up well enough that the bait never backfires on you.

items.title: Wait a moment before a forced move
items.text: Waiting a few seconds before a forced move can look like you are playing casually, which tempts your opponent to capture carelessly.
items.check: Not a chess principle but gamesmanship. Use it sparingly, never waste your clock, and do not rely on it. It is also a draft until we agree it belongs in a chess library.
items.scenario: Try this: when a recapture or an only-move seems forced, still count to five and look at the whole board once. Check whether there is an in-between move or a stronger alternative, and whether the opponent's last move set a trap.

items.title: Win or learn
items.text: Do not let a missed chance or a lost game spoil your enjoyment. Analyze the missed tactics calmly afterwards (such as hidden rook traps or missed in-between moves) to come back stronger.
items.check: Not a chess rule but a useful mindset. Wording: the source said the loss should not "increase" your fun; I read it as "spoil".
items.scenario: Try this: finish every session with one line: "I won" or "I learned: ...". Never write "I lost". It keeps your attention on the lesson, and over a month your notes turn into a personal list of the principles you still need to train.

items.title: Set a fixed number of games per session
items.text: Decide before you start how many games you will play, and stick to it. This stops you from playing on out of frustration or revenge after a loss (tilt) and keeps you fresh and focused.
items.check: Checked: standard advice. Softened: the exact number is personal; a stop-loss rule (such as stopping after two losses in a row) is a good addition.
items.scenario: Try this: before you open the app, write down "3 games" (or any number that fits your evening). After game 3 you stop, even after a loss, and use the last 10 minutes to review your worst game instead. Notice how often the 4th game you were tempted to play would have been played on tilt.

items.title: Set a loss budget
items.text: Accept that you will lose roughly as often as you win against opponents of your own strength. Losses are your best teachers. Expecting them helps you recover faster and brood less.
items.check: Corrected: "about 50%" only holds against similarly rated opponents, which rating systems aim for. Against stronger players you lose more.
items.scenario: Try this: expect that out of every 10 games against similar opponents about 4 to 5 are losses. Count them in your head as "budget spent", not as failure. When you reach your budget for the day, review one loss and call it a successful session.

items.title: Understanding is not the same as executing
items.text: Understanding a master move or plan in a video does not mean you can play it yourself over the board. Mistakes happen at every level, even among grandmasters, so keep training.
items.check: Checked.
items.scenario: Try this: after watching a master game or a lesson, close the video and set up the key position on a board. Play the idea from memory against an engine or a friend. If you cannot find it yet, you understood it but have not trained it. Repeat on three different days.

items.title: Choose a growth mindset
items.text: Do not identify with your results. Enjoy the process of improving your visualisation, calculation and pattern recognition more than the score.
items.check: Checked: well supported in learning research.
items.scenario: Try this: after each game write down one thing you did better than last week, win or lose. Track that list instead of only your rating. Over a month the list shows progress that the rating hides.

items.title: Analyse your lost and difficult games
items.text: Real curiosity shows after the game. If you skip analysis and only play for points, you miss the chance to improve in a structural way and to see where the position went wrong.
items.check: Checked. This is exactly what the game report is for.
items.scenario: Try this: after a loss, run it through the Throiy Chess analyzer. Find the first move where the evaluation dropped most, ask what you were thinking, and write one sentence on what you will check next time. One game analysed this way beats five games played on tilt.

items.title: Stay calm against an unfamiliar early gambit
items.text: Do not panic against a strange or rare gambit. Often you can take the offered pawn, solidify (for example with c3) and send your pieces back to safe squares.
items.check: Softened: "take the pawn" is not always right. First check that the pawn is not poisoned and that you are not falling behind in development.
items.scenario: Try this: when your opponent offers a pawn on move 3 or 4 with a move you do not know, take a minute. Check what the offered pawn opens (lines to your king, pins), and decide whether you can take and then return it if needed while developing. Calm development usually beats trying to refute it from memory.

items.title: Make the opponent's life uncomfortable
items.text: You do not always need the very best computer move. Among good moves, prefer the one that is practically and psychologically hardest for the opponent. Ask questions with active, provocative moves that test the defence.
items.check: Softened: pick among sound moves only. A move that is objectively bad is not "provocative", it is just a mistake.
items.scenario: Try this: when two moves are about equally good, pick the one that asks your opponent a harder question, such as the one with a direct threat or a pin. Opponents under time pressure find it much harder to answer concrete questions than to play quiet moves.

items.title: Create confusion with a complicating sacrifice
items.text: Complicating sacrifices are a practical weapon only when you have checked that they are at worst objectively playable.
items.check: Softened: this is a practical choice for human opponents and not a rule against engines. Only do it when the sacrifice is at worst roughly balanced; a bad sacrifice just loses material.
items.scenario: Try this: before you sacrifice to complicate, play the main lines to the end: can the opponent safely give the material back or reach a draw? If the worst case is still acceptable, the complication is a practical weapon. If the worst case loses by force, do not play it.
